points: Many tree questions are really about levels: the widest level, each level's total, the deepest level. Keep each level's nodes together, then answer the question once per level.
A per-level walk visits each node once: O(n) time. The queue holds about one level at a time: O(width) memory.
Test on an empty tree, one node, and a tree whose left side is deeper than its right.

binary-tree-right-side-view: Stand to the right of the tree and look left: how many nodes do you see on each level, and which one? How would you know it while you walk that level?
Can a node on the left ever show? Draw a tree where one does before you code.

blocks.say: For any per-level question I run BFS and read len(queue) when a level starts, so I know which nodes belong to it; for the right side view I keep the last node of each level, O(n) time and O(width) memory.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): which level of a tree holds the most nodes? Root 1 has children 2 and 3; 2 has children 4 and 5; 3 has a right child 6; 4 has a left child 7.
Queue [1]. Level 0 starts with 1 node in the queue: pop it, push 2 and 3. Best so far: level 0, with 1 node.
Level 1 starts with 2 nodes: pop 2 and 3, push 4, 5 and 6. Level 1 has 2, the new best.
Level 2 starts with 3 nodes: pop 4, 5 and 6, push 7. 3 beats 2, so level 2 is the best. Level 3 has only 7.
Answer: level 2, with 3 nodes. Reading len(queue) before each level's loop kept the levels apart, and each node went in and out of the queue once: O(n).

blocks.title: Normalisation: 1NF to 3NF, and when to denormalise
blocks.builds_on: Day 20 · SQL tables, keys and indexes, and running SQL from Python with sqlite3, and Day 54 · SQL joins and GROUP BY
points: Normalisation means storing each fact once. A table that repeats a fact, such as a restaurant's phone number on every order line, can end up disagreeing with itself.

Three anomalies show the cost. Update: change the phone on some rows and the others keep the old number. Delete: delete a restaurant's only order and the restaurant is gone too. Insert: you can't add a new restaurant until someone orders from it.
1NF: each cell holds one value, and a key tells the rows apart. A column "items" holding "Masala Dosa, Filter Coffee" breaks it: make one row per item.

2NF: when the key has two columns, every other column depends on the whole key, not on part of it. In order lines keyed by (order_id, item), the quantity depends on both, but the customer depends on order_id alone, so the customer moves to an orders table.

3NF: no column depends on another column that isn't the key. The restaurant's phone depends on the restaurant, not on the order, so it moves to a restaurants table. The summary to say: every column depends on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key.

Joins (Day 54) put the pieces back together for reads, and that costs time on every read. Read-heavy systems sometimes denormalise: copy the restaurant's name onto each order, or keep a running total, and accept that every write must keep the copy in step, in the same transaction (Day 20).
Denormalise only a measured, frequent, slow read. And some copies aren't denormalisation at all: the price an order was paid at is its own fact, and must not change when the menu does.
blocks.say: I normalise so each fact lives in one place, up to 3NF, where every column depends on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key; I denormalise only a measured hot read, and keep the copy in step in the same transaction.
example: orders_flat, one row per item (order_id, customer, restaurant, phone, item, qty, price): (1, Asha, Dosa Corner, 080-1111, Masala Dosa, 2, 120), (1, Asha, Dosa Corner, 080-1111, Filter Coffee, 2, 40), (2, Ravi, Dosa Corner, 080-1111, Masala Dosa, 1, 120), (3, Meera, Biryani House, 040-2222, Veg Biryani, 1, 250), (3, Meera, Biryani House, 040-2222, Raita, 2, 30).

It is in 1NF: one value per cell, key (order_id, item). It isn't in 2NF: customer, restaurant and phone depend on order_id alone. Move them to orders(order_id, customer, restaurant, phone): 3 rows. The price is what this order paid, so it stays on the line.

orders isn't in 3NF: the phone depends on the restaurant, a column that isn't the key. Move it to restaurants(name, phone): 2 rows, and orders keeps (order_id, customer, restaurant). order_items(order_id, item, qty, price) keeps 5 rows.
The update anomaly is gone: Dosa Corner's new number is one UPDATE of one row. In the flat table, updating only order 1's rows leaves Dosa Corner with two different phones.
A join with GROUP BY gives back each order's total, SUM(qty × price): 320, 120 and 310, the same as from the flat table.

blocks.title: DSA mock 1: one coding problem with an interviewer
blocks.builds_on: Days 54 to 60 · Trees, and Day 6 · trees and graphs
points: Solving alone trains finding the answer. An interview also scores how you get there: clarifying the question, thinking out loud, taking a hint well and testing your own code. A mock practises those, every Friday this month, one kind of interview at a time. Mock 1 is deliberately close to this week's topic, a tree walked level by level, so the interview itself is the new part; Day 89's is further from what you've just practised.

Set it up like the real thing: a blank file, no notes, and type your thinking into the chat in short lines as you go, the way you would say it out loud. 35 minutes for the problem, then a 10-minute debrief that starts with submitting on LeetCode.
Stuck for about 5 minutes? Ask for a hint. It takes half a point off the area it helped, which is still far better than freezing: interviewers want to see you use help well.

The score: five areas, one point each, 1 if done well, 0.5 if partly, 0 if missed (the checkpoints' scale). Clarifying questions and edge cases; approach and Big-O before code; working code; testing by trace; talking throughout.
Log "Mock 1 (DSA): x/5 · the one thing to fix" in My notes. Day 89's DSA mock compares with it.
blocks.say: In a coding interview I restate the problem with an example, ask about edge cases, give my approach and its Big-O before I code, talk while I code, and finish by tracing a small test through my code.

tasks.text: Paste this into an AI chat of your choice, start a 35-minute timer, and type your thinking into the chat in short lines as you go, the way you would say it out loud: "You are a strict but fair interviewer for an SDE2 role at an Indian product company. Before I code, ask for my approach and its time and space complexity, and push back if it is wrong or vague. When I say I'm done, I will paste my code; judge working code from what I paste, then ask me to trace a small test through it. At the end, score me out of 5, one point per area, 1, 0.5 or 0: clarifying questions and edge cases; approach and Big-O before code; working code; testing by trace; talking throughout. Wait for my first reply."

selftest.q: In BFS on a tree, how do you keep one level's nodes apart from the next level's?
selftest.a: Read len(queue) when a level starts and pop exactly that many nodes; the children pushed meanwhile wait for the next level.

selftest.q: Say 1NF, 2NF and 3NF in one line each.
selftest.a: 1NF: one value per cell and a key. 2NF: no column depends on only part of a two-column key. 3NF: no column depends on another non-key column. Every column depends on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key.

selftest.q: A restaurant's phone is stored on every order line. Name the three anomalies.
selftest.a: Update: changing some rows leaves two phones for one restaurant. Delete: deleting its only order loses the restaurant. Insert: a new restaurant can't be added until someone orders.

selftest.q: When is denormalising worth it, and what do you owe in return?
selftest.a: For a measured, frequent, slow read, usually on data that rarely changes. In return every write must keep the copy in step, in the same transaction.

selftest.q: Re-take from Day 46: what problem does the outbox pattern solve?
selftest.a: Saving a row and publishing an event can't be one transaction across the database and the queue. Write the event into an outbox table in the same database transaction, and a relay publishes it, so neither is lost.

blocks.title: Trees: building a tree from a grid
blocks.builds_on: Day 57 · Trees, and Day 5 · recursion and the call stack
points: Some grid questions split a square into four equal quarters and handle each quarter the same way, down to single cells. Merge sort (Day 11) split a list in two; this splits a square in four.
Each call needs only the square's top-left corner and its side length, (row, col, size). The quarters start at offsets of size ÷ 2, so no sub-grid is ever copied.

Checking every cell of a square again at every level costs O(n² log n) on an n × n grid. Letting the four quarters answer first and combining their answers, as Day 57's subtrees did, looks at each cell once: O(n²).

construct-quad-tree: What makes a square a leaf, and what does its node hold then? What do the four children of a non-leaf stand for?
Once the four quarters are built, when can you throw them away and return a single leaf instead?

blocks.say: For Construct Quad Tree I recurse on (row, col, size), build the four quarters first, and if all four are leaves with the same value I return one leaf instead, so each cell is looked at once, O(n²).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): sum a 4 × 4 grid by quarters, each call taking (row, col, size). The rows: 1 2 0 0 / 3 4 0 1 / 5 5 2 2 / 5 5 2 2.
sum(0, 0, 4): the size isn't 1, so half = 2, and call the four quarters (0, 0, 2), (0, 2, 2), (2, 0, 2) and (2, 2, 2).
The top-left quarter splits into four 1 × 1 cells, the base case: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. The other quarters give 0 + 0 + 0 + 1 = 1, 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20 and 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8.
Total 10 + 1 + 20 + 8 = 39, in 1 + 4 + 16 = 21 calls: two levels of halving below the top, log₂ 4 = 2.
The calls form a tree with four children per node, and each answer is built from the four below it, the way Day 57's answers came up from two subtrees.

blocks.title: Linked List (hard): Reverse Nodes in k-Group
blocks.builds_on: Days 39 to 45 · Linked List
first: Timer: 40 minutes. Stuck when it rings: one line in My notes on where, then take the help on its row one step at a time. Show the answer last and watch only the idea in its Video, then close it and code it from blank. Show the answer turns its bookmark on for you.
points: You reversed a whole list (Day 39) and part of a list between two positions (Day 44), with a dummy head in front. This hard does a part-reversal again and again along the list.

reverse-nodes-in-k-group: Step 1, by hand: take 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 with k = 2 and write the list after each group. Which nodes does one group's reversal need to know: the node before the group, the group's first and last nodes, the node after it?
Step 2: before you reverse a group, how do you check that k nodes are left? What happens to a last group shorter than k?
Step 3: after one group is reversed, its old first node is its last. Which two links must you fix so the group joins the list on both sides, and which node is 'the node before' the next group?
Step 4: what special case does a dummy head in front save you for the first group? Trace k = 3 on 1 → 2 → … → 8, and count how many times each node is touched: what are the time and the extra memory?

blocks.say: I put a dummy head in front, check that k nodes remain, reverse that group in place with three pointers, then link the node before the group to its new first node and its old first node to what follows, and move on: O(n) time and O(1) extra memory, with a short last group left as it is.
example: Practice problem (not NeetCode 250): rotate a list right by k places. 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 with k = 2 becomes 4 → 5 → 1 → 2 → 3.
Walk once to find the length, 5, and the tail, node 5. Rotating by 7 is the same as by 7 mod 5 = 2, so take k mod length first; if it is 0, return the list unchanged.
The new tail is length − k − 1 = 2 steps from the head: node 3. The new head is the node after it: node 4.
Re-link in three moves: old tail 5 → old head 1, new tail 3 → None, head = 4. Result: 4 → 5 → 1 → 2 → 3, in O(n) time and O(1) memory.
The habit for list hards: find the few boundary nodes first (before, first, last, after), write them down, then change the links in an order that never loses a node you still need.

blocks.title: Design a notification system: push, SMS and email, with retries and limits
blocks.builds_on: Day 39 · message queues, at-least-once delivery, retries and dead-letter queues, Day 18 · API design and idempotency keys, Day 46 · the outbox pattern, Day 48 · rate limiting, Day 60 · live updates, and Day 32 · the 45-minute design framework
points: The ask: other services (orders, payments, marketing) call one service to tell a user something by push, SMS or email. An order update must arrive in seconds, a campaign to 10 million users may take minutes, and an OTP can never wait behind the campaign.

Start with Day 32's framework: users, notifications a day, the peak, the channels, and how fast each kind must arrive. 20 million users × 5 a day is 100 million a day, about 1,200 a second on average.

API: send(user_id, type, data, idempotency_key). The service looks up the user's preferences (SMS switched off? quiet hours?) and contact details, fills the template for that type in the user's language, and picks the channels.

A queue per channel and priority (Day 39): OTPs and order updates in one, campaigns in another, so a slow email provider or a big campaign can't hold up an OTP. Workers on each queue call the provider: APNs or FCM for push, an SMS gateway, an email service. A push reaches a phone even with the app closed, unlike Day 60's WebSocket, which needs the app open.
Providers time out. Retry with exponential backoff (1, 2, 4, 8 seconds, plus a little random jitter), cap the tries, then move the message to a dead-letter queue (Day 39) for someone to look at.

At-least-once delivery means a retry can send twice. Dedup with the idempotency key (Day 18): keep the keys already accepted, with an expiry, and drop a repeat. Today's optional guide lab (about 30 minutes) practises exactly this, if the block leaves time.
Per-user rate limits (Day 48): at most a few promotional messages per user an hour or a day, so a bug or a campaign can't spam anyone. OTPs and order updates skip the limit.

Tracking: each notification's status (queued, sent, delivered, opened, failed) in a store keyed by its id; providers report delivery back by webhook, a call to a URL of ours. The outbox (Day 46) makes "order saved" and "notification requested" happen together.
blocks.say: A notification service takes send requests with an idempotency key, checks preferences and per-user limits, fills a template and queues the message per channel and priority; workers call the push, SMS and email providers with backoff retries and a dead-letter queue, and every status is tracked.
example: Asha has push and email on and SMS off; promotions are limited to 3 an hour, and order updates skip the limit. At t = 0 s, a promotion by push, key p1: queued.
t = 5: the marketing service retries the same call with key p1: duplicate, dropped. A promotion by SMS at t = 5: opted out.

t = 10 and t = 20: promotions by push and by email, both queued, 3 in the last hour. t = 30: a fourth promotion: rate limited, though an order update by push at t = 31 still goes through. t = 3,610: the promotions from t = 0 and t = 10 are at least an hour old, so the next one is queued.
The push provider fails twice: tries at t = 0 and t = 1 fail, and the retry at t = 3 (after waits of 1 and 2 seconds) delivers.
A provider that stays down: tries at t = 0, 1, 3, 7 and 15 all fail, and after the fifth the message goes to the dead-letter queue.

blocks.title: Trees: comparing a node with the nodes above it
blocks.builds_on: Days 54 to 62 · Trees, and Day 5 · recursion and the call stack
points: Day 57's answers flowed up: each subtree reported to its parent. Some questions need the opposite: a node must know something about the path above it, such as its depth or the largest value so far.
Pass that down as a parameter: the first call starts it, and each call hands its children an updated value. Nothing needs undoing on the way back, because every call has its own copy.
Many problems use both directions: information goes down as parameters, and counts come back up as return values, or into a nonlocal total (Day 58).

count-good-nodes-in-binary-tree: What does a node need to know about the nodes above it to decide whether it is good? Can that fit in one number?
What is that number for the root, and how does it change for each child?

blocks.say: For Count Good Nodes I run a DFS that carries the largest value on the path so far; a node is good if it is at least that value, and I pass max(that value, node.val) to both children: O(n) time, O(h) memory.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): count the nodes whose value equals their depth, with the root at depth 0. Root 0; its left child 1 has children 2 and 7; its right child 5 has a left child 2.
count(node, depth): None gives 0. Otherwise (1 if node.val == depth else 0) + count(left, depth + 1) + count(right, depth + 1). Start with count(root, 0).
Down the left: 0 at depth 0 matches, 1 at depth 1 matches, 2 at depth 2 matches, 7 at depth 2 doesn't.
Down the right: 5 at depth 1 doesn't match; its child 2 at depth 2 does. Total 4.
The depth went down as a parameter and the counts came back up as return values. Each node is visited once: O(n) time, O(h) memory.

blocks.title: Stack (hard): Maximum Frequency Stack
blocks.builds_on: Days 46 to 53 · Stack, and Day 49 · designing a structure whose every operation is O(1)
first: Timer: 40 minutes. Stuck when it rings: one line in My notes on where, then take the help on its row one step at a time. Show the answer last and watch only the idea in its Video, then close it and code it from blank. Show the answer turns its bookmark on for you.
points: You kept a running answer beside a stack (Day 49) and grouped keys by how often they were used (Day 49's hard). This hard combines counting with a stack's last-in, first-out order.

maximum-frequency-stack: Step 1, brute force: keep a plain list. For pop, count every value, find the highest count, and remove the most recent value that has it. What does one pop cost?
Step 2: keep a dict of value → count, updated on push and pop, so a value's count is O(1). What else must you find fast: the highest count, and which value with that count was pushed last?

Step 3: think of a 5 pushed three times as three copies, its 1st, 2nd and 3rd. If you grouped every copy by that number, what would the group with the highest number look like, and which end should pop take from?
Step 4: when that group empties after a pop, what is the new highest count, and can you know it without searching? Trace push 5, 7, 5, 7, 4, 5, then four pops: 5, 7, 5, 4.

blocks.say: I keep a count per value and a stack per count: push raises x's count to c and pushes x onto stack c; pop takes from the stack of the highest count, lowers that value's count, and drops the highest count by one when its stack empties, so both are O(1).
example: Practice problem (not NeetCode 250, LeetCode 451): sort the letters of "banana" by how often they appear, most frequent first: "aaannb".

Count with a dict: a 3, n 2, b 1. Then bucket by count, as in Day 13's O(n) answer to Top K Frequent. No count can be more than the word's length, 6, so make buckets[0] to buckets[6], one list per count.
Append each letter to the list of its count, O(1) each: buckets[3] = [a], buckets[2] = [n], buckets[1] = [b]. Walk from 6 down to 1 and write each letter count times: aaannb.
Counting is O(n) and each bucket is reached by its index, so there is no sorting at all: O(n) in total. Grouping by count turns "the most frequent" into "the highest bucket that isn't empty".
Here every count was known before the walk. If the counts changed one at a time while you answered, how far could the highest non-empty bucket move after one change?

blocks.title: Machine coding: a coffee machine with add-ons, custom orders and low-stock alerts
blocks.builds_on: Day 51 · Decorator, Day 58 · Builder, Day 37 · the State pattern, Day 30 · the Observer pattern, Day 42 · the vending machine and its safe sale order, and Day 21 · the machine-coding playbook and enums
points: A 90-minute machine-coding round in Day 21's shape: 10 minutes for requirements, entities and states, then build in slices that run, then tests and a demo. Four patterns you've met each have a natural place here; say why you picked each. Today's optional guide lab (about 30 minutes) is for a day with time left over.

Requirements: drinks (Espresso ₹80, Latte ₹120) with add-ons in any mix (extra shot +₹30, caramel +₹25); take payment and give change; track coffee, water, milk and caramel; refuse a drink the stock can't make; alert staff when an ingredient runs low.
Add-ons are Decorators (Day 51): ExtraShot(Latte()) has the same price() and recipe() as a drink and adds its own part. Two shots are ExtraShot(ExtraShot(Latte())), with no LatteWithTwoShots class.

A custom order on a touch screen arrives one tap at a time, so a Builder (Day 58) collects the drink and its add-ons, and build() checks the rules, such as at most two extra shots, before wrapping the decorators.
The machine is Day 37's State pattern: Idle, then AwaitingPayment once a drink is chosen, then back to Idle after brewing or a cancel. Paying while Idle says "choose a drink first".
The inventory is a subject (Day 30): staff screens subscribe, and each gets one alert when an ingredient drops below its threshold, not one on every cup after.
Brew in Day 42's safe order: check every ingredient first, then take them all, then give change. A refused drink takes nothing and refunds in full.
Extensions to discuss: a new add-on (one class), card or UPI payments (a Strategy, Day 16), and a cleaning cycle (one more state).
blocks.say: I model add-ons as decorators over a Beverage interface, build custom orders with a builder that validates them, run the machine as a State pattern, and have the inventory notify observers once when stock crosses a threshold; a drink checks every ingredient before it takes any.
example: A Latte is ₹120 and takes 18 g coffee, 30 ml water and 150 ml milk. An extra shot adds ₹30, 18 g coffee and 30 ml water; caramel adds ₹25 and 15 ml caramel.
Caramel(ExtraShot(Latte())): price() asks the drink inside and adds its own: 120 + 30 + 25 = ₹175. recipe() gives 36 g coffee, 60 ml water, 150 ml milk and 15 ml caramel.
Stock: 100 g coffee, with an alert below 40 g. A latte with an extra shot takes 36 g: 64 g left, no alert. A second: 28 g left, which crosses below 40, so one alert.
A third needs 36 g but only 28 g is left: it is refused before anything is taken, so the milk and water stay as they were and the money goes back.
The machine: choose the drink, so Idle → AwaitingPayment; pay ₹200 for the ₹175 drink: it brews, gives ₹25 change and goes back to Idle.

blocks.title: Word order: positional encodings and RoPE
blocks.builds_on: Day 59 · the transformer block, and why attention alone can't see word order, Day 57 · masked multi-head attention, Day 52 · attention as softmax of q·k scores, and Day 49 · embedding tables
points: Day 59's promise: attention alone treats "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" alike, because it only compares vectors and no vector says where its token sits. The fix: give each position a vector and add it to the token's vector before the first block.

Learnt positions (GPT-2): a second embedding table with one row per position, up to the longest input (1,024 rows of 768 numbers in GPT-2 small), trained like the token table (Day 49). Simple, but it knows nothing past position 1,023.

Fixed sines and cosines (the original transformer): PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d)) and PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^(2i/d)). Each pair of columns is a clock turning at its own speed: at d = 16 the fastest repeats every 6.3 positions, the slowest about every 20,000.

Why it works: the dot product of two position vectors depends only on how far apart they are. At d = 16, PE[5]·PE[7] = PE[20]·PE[22] = 6.37, so "two words apart" looks the same anywhere in the sentence. Nothing to learn, and any length works.
The position vector has the same size d as the token vector and is added to it, not joined on, so the shape stays n × d (Day 59).

RoPE, rotary positions (Llama and most new models): instead of adding to x, rotate each pair of numbers in q and k by an angle proportional to the token's position, just before the scores. Rotating q by m·θ and k by n·θ leaves their dot product depending only on m − n, so the score sees the distance directly.
In 2-D with θ = 0.5: q = k = [1, 0] at positions 3 and 1 score cos(1) = 0.54, and at positions 13 and 11 exactly the same. Without positions both pairs would score 1, blind to order.
blocks.say: Attention can't see order, so we inject position: GPT-2 adds a learnt position embedding, the original transformer adds fixed sines and cosines at many frequencies, and RoPE rotates q and k by position-dependent angles so that their score depends only on the distance between the tokens.
example: The sin/cos table for d = 4: columns 0 and 1 use pos / 10000^0 = pos; columns 2 and 3 use pos / 10000^(2/4) = pos / 100.
Position 0: [sin 0, cos 0, sin 0, cos 0] = [0, 1, 0, 1].
The fast pair changes a lot from one position to the next and the slow pair barely moves; together they give every position its own pattern, like a clock's second and hour hands.
RoPE in 2-D with θ = 0.5: q = [2, 1] at position 5 and k = [1, 3] at position 2 score 5.341; at positions 105 and 102 the score is again 5.341. Their plain dot product is 5.

blocks.builds_on: Days 54 to 63 · Trees, and Day 59 · binary search trees
points: Day 59's BST rule is about whole subtrees: every value in the left subtree is smaller than the node, and every value in the right subtree is larger. A check of each node against only its own two children misses a value deep down on the wrong side of a grandparent.
Test on one node, a tree holding two equal values, and values at the very ends of the integer range.

valid-binary-search-tree: Draw a tree where every node is correct against its own two children, yet it isn't a BST. What did the check miss?
Every node sits below some of its ancestors and above others. So what range of values is it allowed, where does each end of that range come from, and what is the root's range?
kth-smallest-integer-in-bst: Which traversal order of a BST (Day 54) hands you the values smallest first?
How do you stop that walk once you have counted k, rather than walking the whole tree, and what does it cost then?

blocks.say: To validate a BST I pass each node the open range (low, high) its ancestors allow and narrow it on the way down; for the k-th smallest I walk inorder with my own stack and stop at the k-th pop, O(h + k) time.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list, LeetCode 938): sum the values from 7 to 15 in a BST. Root 10; left child 5 with children 3 and 7; right child 15 with a right child 18.
At 10: in range, add 10. Its left subtree holds values below 10, and 10 > 7, so some could be in range: go left. Its right subtree holds values above 10, and 10 < 15: go right too.
At 5: out of range. Everything to its left is below 5, and 5 isn't above 7, so skip that whole subtree, the 3, unseen. Go right to 7: in range, add 7.
At 15: in range, add 15. Everything to its right is above 15, so skip the 18. Its left is empty.
Total 10 + 7 + 15 = 32, having visited 4 of the 6 nodes. The BST rule let the walk skip a subtree whole, without looking inside it.

blocks.builds_on: Day 63 · position embeddings, Day 59 · the transformer block with residuals and layer norm, Day 57 · masked multi-head attention, Day 49 · nn.Embedding, nn.Linear, .view and cross_entropy, and Day 45 · sampling with torch.multinomial
points: nanoGPT's model.py is GPT-2 in about 330 lines, and you have built every piece of it. Read it as four classes, CausalSelfAttention, MLP, Block and GPT, then GPT's generate method.

CausalSelfAttention: one Linear, c_attn, makes q, k and v together and splits them in three. `.view(B, T, n_head, head_size)` cuts each token's columns into heads, Day 57's column slices, and `.transpose(1, 2)` moves the head axis forward so every head works as its own batch. scaled_dot_product_attention with is_causal=True is Day 57's masked softmax(q·kᵀ / √head_size)·v in one call; c_proj is Day 57's W_o, mixing the heads back together.
MLP: a Linear up to 4 × n_embd, GELU (a smooth ReLU), and a Linear back down. Block: x = x + attn(ln_1(x)), then x = x + mlp(ln_2(x)), Day 59's pre-norm.

GPT: wte is the token table and wpe the learnt position table (Day 63). x = wte(idx) + wpe(positions), then the blocks, then a last layer norm, ln_f. GPT-2's 50,257 tokens are padded to 50,304, a multiple of 64 that runs faster.

Weight tying: `self.transformer.wte.weight = self.lm_head.weight` makes the output layer share the token table, so the logits are ln_f(x) @ wteᵀ: a token's score is how well the final vector matches that token's own embedding. In GPT-2 small it saves 50,304 × 768 ≈ 38.6 million weights.
forward with targets gives logits for every position and the cross-entropy loss (Day 49); without targets it computes the logits for the last position only, all that generation needs.

generate: crop the input to block_size, run forward, take the last position's logits, divide by the temperature (below 1 sharpens the probabilities, above 1 flattens them), optionally keep the top_k (only the k likeliest tokens), softmax, and pick with torch.multinomial (Day 45); append and repeat. Day 71 goes deeper. Deep-ML #88 takes the argmax instead, which always picks the likeliest token.
blocks.say: nanoGPT is GPT-2 in one file: token plus learnt position embeddings, a stack of pre-norm blocks of causal multi-head attention and a GELU MLP with residuals, a final layer norm, and an output layer tied to the token table; generate samples the next token from the last position's softmax and repeats.
example: A tiny config: block_size 8, vocab 65 (Shakespeare's characters), 2 layers, 4 heads, n_embd 32. It prints 0.03M parameters: 27,552, because get_num_params leaves out wpe's 8 × 32 = 256.
idx of shape (4, 8): 4 sequences of 8 token ids. wte(idx) is (4, 8, 32) and wpe(arange(8)) is (8, 32); adding them broadcasts the positions to every sequence: (4, 8, 32).
Inside attention: c_attn gives (4, 8, 96), split into q, k and v of (4, 8, 32); each is viewed as (4, 8, 4, 8) and transposed to (4, 4, 8, 8), 4 heads of size 8. The output goes back to (4, 8, 32).
Both blocks keep (4, 8, 32). Then ln_f and lm_head: logits (4, 8, 65) with targets, and a loss of about 4.19 at the start, near ln 65 = 4.17 for even guessing.
Without targets: logits (4, 1, 65), the last position only. generate(idx[:, :3], 5) appends 5 sampled tokens to 3: shape (4, 8).

points: Both problems are recursion on subtrees: each call handles one root and trusts the calls on its subtrees. Decide first what each call takes in and what it hands back.

binary-tree-from-preorder-and-inorder-tr: One order alone can't rebuild a tree: Day 54's (2 + 3) × 4 lost its brackets in inorder. Which of today's two lists tells you the root at once, and what does the other list tell you about what lies to its left and right?
Once you know where the root sits in inorder, how big is the left subtree, and which parts of each list belong to it? Could you pass index ranges instead of slices, so nothing is copied?
Scanning the inorder list for each root costs O(n) per node. What could you build once, before the recursion, to find it in O(1)?
house-robber-iii: Try returning one number per subtree, its best total. Can the parent decide whether to take itself from that number alone? What is missing?

The best total depends on a choice at each root: take it or not. What if each call returned a small tuple, one answer per choice? How would a parent build its pair from its children's pairs (Day 7's first feel for dynamic programming)?

blocks.say: For preorder plus inorder I take the next preorder value as the root, find its inorder index in a dict to split the left and right ranges, and recurse, O(n); for House Robber III each node returns two totals, with itself and without, and the parent combines them, O(n).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list, LeetCode 108): build a balanced BST from the sorted list [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7].
build(lo, hi) on index ranges: if lo > hi, return None. Otherwise take mid = (lo + hi) // 2 as the root, then root.left = build(lo, mid − 1) and root.right = build(mid + 1, hi).
build(0, 6): middle value 4. Left, build(0, 2): middle 2, with children 1 and 3. Right, build(4, 6): middle 6, with children 5 and 7.
Preorder of the result: 4 2 1 3 6 5 7, height 2. Every value lands on the correct side, because the left range holds only smaller values and the right range only larger ones.
Each value becomes a node once: O(n) time. Passing (lo, hi) instead of slicing avoids copying the list at every level.

blocks.title: Command pattern: actions as objects, with undo
blocks.builds_on: Day 16 · Strategy and objects that share one small interface, Days 46 to 53 · Stack, and Day 51 · Decorator and Composite
points: Command: wrap a request in an object with `execute()` and `undo()`. The caller, the invoker, runs commands without knowing what they do, the way Day 16's strategies share one interface.
Once an action is an object you can keep it: queue it to run later, log it, retry it, or undo it.
Undo is a stack (Day 46): the invoker pushes each command after it runs, and undo pops the last one and calls its undo(). Redo is a second stack: undo pushes onto it, and any new command clears it.
Each command keeps what it needs to reverse itself: a transfer keeps the two accounts and the amount; "delete line 3" keeps the line's text.
Push only a command that actually ran: a transfer refused for low balance must not land on the undo stack, or undo would hand back money that was never sent.
Command vs Strategy: a strategy is how one job is done, swapped in (Day 16); a command is one particular request, with its own data, that can be stored and reversed.
Where you've seen it: Ctrl+Z in an editor, the tasks on a job queue (Day 39), and database migrations with up and down steps.
blocks.say: The Command pattern turns each action into an object with execute and undo; an invoker runs it and pushes it on an undo stack, so undo pops and reverses the last one, redo uses a second stack, and commands can also be queued, logged or retried.
example: A Paytm-like wallet: Asha has ₹1,000 and Ravi ₹500. Transfer(asha, ravi, 300) runs: ₹700 and ₹800. The invoker pushes it.
Transfer(ravi, asha, 200) runs: ₹900 and ₹600, pushed. The undo stack holds both.
Transfer(asha, ravi, 5000) is refused for low balance and never pushed: still ₹900 and ₹600.
Undo pops the second transfer and calls its undo(): ₹700 and ₹800. Undo again: ₹1,000 and ₹500. A third undo finds the stack empty and does nothing.
Redo pops the first transfer off the redo stack and runs it again: ₹700 and ₹800.

selftest.q: Preorder [3, 9, 20, 15, 7] and inorder [9, 3, 15, 20, 7]: what is the root, and which values are in its left subtree?

selftest.q: In House Robber III, why can't each subtree return just its best total?

selftest.q: How does the Command pattern support undo and redo?
selftest.a: Each command keeps what it needs to reverse itself; the invoker pushes commands that ran onto an undo stack. Undo pops one, calls undo() and pushes it onto a redo stack; a new command clears the redo stack.

selftest.a: A strategy is a way of doing one job, swapped in. A command is one specific request with its own data that can be stored, queued, logged and undone.

example: Practice problem (not on today's list, LeetCode 669): trim a BST so only the values from 1 to 3 remain. Root 3; its left child 0 has a right child 2, whose left child is 1; its right child is 4.
trim(node) returns the new root of the trimmed subtree. At 3: in range, so keep it, and set 3.left = trim(0) and 3.right = trim(4).
trim(4): 4 is above 3, so 4 and everything to its right go; anything in range would sit in its left subtree, which is empty: return None.
trim(0): 0 is below 1, so 0 and everything to its left go; return trim(2). At 2: in range, keep it, and 2.left = trim(1), which is 1. So trim(0) returns 2, and 3.left becomes 2.
Result: 3, with left child 2, whose left child is 1. Returning each subtree's new root let every parent re-link without knowing what changed below. O(n) time.

blocks.title: Tokenisation: BPE, and how tokens drive cost and context
blocks.builds_on: Day 45 · characters as tokens in the bigram model, Day 49 · the embedding table, one row per token, and Day 64 · GPT-2's vocabulary of 50,257 tokens in nanoGPT
points: Today's guide lesson (about 20 minutes) covers what a tokenizer is made of and what changing one costs, so the block's own reading is short.

Models see token ids, not letters. Characters (Day 45) make sequences long; whole words make the vocabulary huge and can't handle a new word. Subwords sit between: a common word is one token, a rare one splits into pieces.

Byte-pair encoding (BPE) learns the pieces: first split the training text into words (the pre-tokenizer, which today's guide lesson covers), so a merge never crosses a word boundary. Within the words, start from single characters (bytes, in GPT models), count every adjacent pair, merge the most frequent pair into a new token, and repeat until the vocabulary is the size you want.
To tokenise new text, apply the learnt merges in the order they were learnt. Vocabulary sizes: GPT-2 50,257; GPT-4's cl100k_base about 100,000; GPT-4o's o200k_base about 200,000.

Tokens are the unit of cost and of context: an API charges per token, and a context window is counted in tokens. "Your order will arrive in 20 minutes." is 9 tokens in both; the same sentence in Hindi is 37 tokens in cl100k_base but 12 in o200k_base, so the bigger vocabulary makes Hindi about 3 times cheaper.
Why models miscount letters: "strawberry" reaches the model as a few pieces, such as str, aw and berry, never as ten letters, so counting its r's asks about letters it never sees directly.
Spaces belong to tokens: " strawberry" with a leading space is a single token in both encodings, while "strawberry" with no space before it is three.
blocks.say: BPE starts from bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token; tokens are the unit of price and context, so a tokenizer that splits Hindi into many pieces makes Hindi users pay several times more, and models miscount letters because they see tokens, not characters.
example: Practice corpus, with word counts: chai 10, chat 6, hat 4, that 3. Start from single letters.
Count adjacent pairs across the corpus, weighted by the counts: h+a appears in all four words, 10 + 6 + 4 + 3 = 23, the most. Merge it into the token ha.
Recount: c+ha is 16 (chai and chat), the most. Merge it into cha: now chai is cha i and chat is cha t.
Recount: cha+i 10, ha+t 7 (hat and that), cha+t 6. Merge cha+i: chai is now one token. The fourth merge is ha+t, at 7.
After four merges: chai and hat are one token each, chat is cha t, and that is t hat. The most frequent words became single tokens; the rarer ones stay in pieces.

blocks.title: Tries: a tree of letters for prefixes
blocks.builds_on: Days 54 to 66 · Trees
first: New topic, Tries, and a new tool. A trie stores words letter by letter in a tree: each node holds a dict from a letter to the child node, and a flag saying whether a word ends there. Words that share a start share its path, so everything with a given prefix hangs below one node.

Insert walks the word from the root, creating a child for each letter that's missing, and marks the last node. Looking up a prefix walks the same way and stops at the first missing letter. Both take O(L) for L letters, however many words are stored.

Practice problem (not on today's list): a phone's contact search, "how many contacts start with as?". Insert each name and add 1 to a count on every node you pass; the answer is the count on the prefix's last node. Insert asha and ashok: the count on s is 2 and on o is 1, so as gives 2 and asho gives 1.
points: Code shape: a TrieNode class that sets `self.children = {}` and `self.end = False` in `__init__`, and a trie that keeps a root node holding no letter.
Memory: one node per distinct prefix. asha, ashok, amit and ravi have 17 letters, but they share a, as and ash, so they need 13 nodes below the root.

implement-prefix-tree: What is the difference between "apple was inserted" and "some word starts with apple"? Which part of a node tells them apart?
design-word-search-data-structure: A '.' can be any letter. At that node, which children must you try, and how do you know when one of them succeeded?
Without dots the walk follows one path. What is the worst case with dots, say a word that is all dots?

blocks.say: A trie node holds a dict of children and an end-of-word flag; insert and prefix search walk one node per letter, O(L); for a '.' wildcard I search depth-first, trying every child at that position and returning True as soon as one branch matches the rest.
example: Insert asha: root → a → s → h → a, all new, with count 1 on each; mark the last a as a word end.
Insert ashok: a, s and h exist, so their counts become 2; o and k are new, with count 1. Insert amit: a's count becomes 3, and m, i and t are new under a. Insert ravi: a new branch from the root.
Prefix as: walk a, then s, and read its count: 2, asha and ashok. ash is also 2, and asho is 1.
Prefix a gives 3 and r gives 1; b stops at once, because the root has no b: 0.
Each query walks one node per letter of the prefix, O(L), whether the phone holds 4 contacts or 4,000. The 17 letters fit in 13 nodes below the root, because shared starts share nodes.

blocks.title: Fan-out: on write vs on read
blocks.builds_on: Day 62 · the notification system's queues and workers, Day 39 · message queues, Day 13 · caching, and Day 41 · sharding and hot keys
points: A feed (Instagram, X, LinkedIn) shows each user the newest posts from everyone they follow. The design question is when to do the work of putting a post in front of its followers.

Fan-out on write, or push: when someone posts, a worker (Day 62's queues and workers) adds the post's id to every follower's feed list in a cache (Day 13). Reading a feed is then one cache read; the cost is that each post becomes one write per follower.
Fan-out on read, or pull: store each post once; when a user opens the app, fetch the latest posts of everyone they follow and merge them by time. Posting is cheap; every read does the work.

The numbers: 100 million daily users, 10 million posts a day, 200 followers on average (so each user also follows about 200), 10 feed opens per user a day. Push: 2 billion feed inserts a day, about 23,000 a second, and 1 billion cheap reads, about 11,600 a second.
Pull on the same numbers: each of the 1 billion opens looks at 200 accounts, 200 billion lookups a day, about 2.3 million a second. Push wins when reads far outnumber posts, as they do in most feeds.

The celebrity problem: one post from an account with 50 million followers is 50 million writes, nearly a minute of work at a million writes a second, for every post. It is a hot key (Day 41) on the write side.

The hybrid most feeds use: push for ordinary accounts; for celebrities, don't fan out, and merge their recent posts in at read time. Skip pushes to users who haven't opened the app in weeks, and build their feed by pull when they return.

Storage: keep only post ids in each feed list, capped at about 500, and fetch the posts themselves from a post cache. 100 million users × 500 ids × 8 bytes is 400 GB of cache, spread over many machines.
blocks.say: Fan-out on write pushes each post id into every follower's cached feed so reads are one lookup, while fan-out on read merges the followed accounts' posts at read time; since reads far outnumber posts I push for ordinary accounts and pull celebrities' posts at read time, the hybrid.
example: Asha follows Ravi, who has 300 followers, and a cricket star with 50 million. Ravi posts at 9:00: a worker pushes the post id into the feed lists of his 300 followers, Asha's included: 300 cache writes.
The star posts at 9:01: no fan-out. The post is stored once, and the account is marked as a celebrity.

Asha opens the app at 9:05: read her feed list, which already holds Ravi's post, fetch the latest posts of the one celebrity she follows, and merge by time: the star's 9:01 post on top, then Ravi's 9:00.
Cost: the star's post took 1 write instead of 50 million, and Asha's read took one list read plus one small lookup per celebrity she follows.
A user who hasn't opened the app in a month gets no pushes. When they return, their feed is built once by pull, then kept up to date by push again.

first: Fridays start with revision, but today's guide reading (about 10 minutes) shares this block, so there are no re-solves today: anything due stays in the Revise row, and Sunday's review starts with it. points: Some string questions ask for the best way to cut a string into pieces. Name the answer for the rest of the string from index i: best(i), the answer for s[i:] alone. The whole answer is best(0), and best(len(s)) is the base case, an empty rest.
best(i) tries each possible first piece and adds best(where that piece ends). Many different cuts reach the same i, so cache best with functools.cache (Day 7): each i is worked out once.

To list every dictionary word that starts at i, walk the trie (Day 67) from its root along s[i], s[i + 1], …: each node with the end-of-word flag is a word ending there, and the walk stops as soon as a character has no child. One walk finds them all, instead of slicing out and looking up every s[i:j].

extra-characters-in-a-string: The character at i is either left over, which costs 1 and leaves best(i + 1), or it starts a dictionary word. Write best(i) as the smaller of those choices.
Say the cost before coding: how many values of i are there, and how far can the trie walk from each one go?

blocks.say: I define best(i) as the fewest leftover characters in s[i:], take the smaller of leaving s[i] over (1 + best(i + 1)) or jumping past each dictionary word that starts at i, which one trie walk from i finds, and cache best so each i is solved once: O(n²) time.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): highlight every product name inside a chat message. The words are buy, red, redmi, mi and phone; the message is "buyredmiphone". List each word found with its start and end index.
Put the five words in a trie. From i = 0, walk b, u, y: y ends a word, so (0, 2) buy. The next letter, r, is not a child of y: stop.
From i = 3, walk r, e, d: (3, 5) red. Keep going, m, i: (3, 7) redmi. Then p is not a child: stop. From i = 4 and i = 5, e and d are not children of the root: stop at once.
From i = 6, m, i gives (6, 7) mi, and from i = 8, p, h, o, n, e gives (8, 12) phone. The other starts stop on their first letter.
Five words found with 15 steps down the trie in all. Each start walks at most to the end of the string, so the worst case is O(n²) steps, and every word that starts at i is found by one walk from i.

blocks.title: Indexes: B+ trees, and when an index hurts
blocks.builds_on: Day 20 · an index is a sorted B-tree with O(log n) lookups, every index costs each write, and a composite index serves its first column, Day 53 · a B-tree updates pages in place, unlike an LSM tree, and Day 54 · SQL from Python with sqlite3
points: Day 20 said an index is a sorted structure, usually a B-tree. Most databases use the B+ tree form: every entry (a key and where its row lives) sits in the leaf pages, in key order, and each leaf links to the next. The pages above hold only keys that steer the search down.

A page is a fixed block, often 8 KB (PostgreSQL) or 16 KB (MySQL), and one branch page holds hundreds of keys. So the tree is very flat: three or four levels cover hundreds of millions of rows, and the top levels stay in memory.

A lookup walks from the root to one leaf, then fetches the row from the table. A range (BETWEEN, >, ORDER BY) finds its first leaf and walks along the linked leaves, never back up the tree. That is why a B+ tree serves ranges, and a hash index serves only equality.

Covering index: when the index holds every column a query needs, the database answers from the index alone and never visits the table. SQLite's plan says COVERING INDEX; PostgreSQL calls it an index-only scan.

Composite index, Day 20's rule made exact: (city, created_at) is sorted by city, then by time inside each city. It serves city = ?, and city = ? AND created_at > ?, but not created_at alone. Put the equality columns first and the range column last.

When an index can't help: the query wraps the column in an expression (lower(email) = …, customer_id + 0 = …), a LIKE starts with a wildcard ('%kumar'), or the query matches a big share of the rows. Each match costs a jump to the table, so for status = 'delivered' on 70% of orders, a planner such as PostgreSQL's reads the whole table in order instead.

When an index hurts: every insert, delete, or update of an indexed column changes each index too, and each one takes disk and memory. Index what the hot queries filter, join and sort by, and drop what nothing uses.
Read the plan instead of guessing: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN in SQLite (EXPLAIN in PostgreSQL and MySQL) says SCAN, every row, or SEARCH … USING INDEX.
blocks.say: Databases index with a B+ tree: three or four levels deep, entries in linked leaves so a range is a walk sideways; I index what the hot queries filter and sort by, equality columns first and the range last, check the plan says SEARCH and not SCAN, and remember every index slows every write.
example: An orders table of 100 million rows with an index on customer_id, in 8 KB pages. A branch entry is a key and a page number, about 16 bytes, so one page points to about 500 pages below it; a leaf holds about 400 entries.

Three levels: one root page points to 500 branch pages, which point to 250,000 leaf pages: 250,000 × 400 = 100 million entries. The root and the 500 branch pages are about 4 MB and stay in memory, so a lookup usually reads one leaf from disk, then the row.
Range: customer_id from 40 to 45. Walk down once to the leaf holding 40, then follow each leaf's link to the next until a key passes 45. Nothing climbs back up the tree.

Each match still costs a jump to the table row, often on a different page. 10 matches is up to 10 more page reads, which is cheap; 30 million matches would be 30 million jumps, so reading the whole table in order wins.
With three indexes on the table, one insert writes the row and an entry in three leaves, now and then splitting a full leaf in two: that is the write cost of an index.

Add `CREATE INDEX idx_customer ON orders(customer_id)` and print it again: `SEARCH orders USING INDEX idx_customer (customer_id=?)`. The query returns 10 rows either way.

Add `CREATE INDEX idx_city_time ON orders(city, created_at)` and print the plans of three queries: `city = 'Pune' AND created_at > 1700500000` (SEARCH, using both columns), `city = 'Pune'` alone (SEARCH, city=?), and `created_at > 1700500000` alone (SCAN: the index is sorted by city first). blocks.title: Backtracking: Sum of All Subsets XOR Total
blocks.builds_on: Day 5 · recursion and its base case, and Days 54 to 60 · Trees
first: Today's guide reading (about 5 minutes) shares this block, so give today's problem about 25 minutes. It opens a new topic and is the plainest example of it: solve it any way you can first, then take the help on its row.
points: Today's new topic, Backtracking: build every possible answer one choice at a time. Draw the choices as a tree: the root is "nothing chosen yet", each level decides one more thing, and each path from the root to a leaf is one complete set of choices.
For "which items do I take?", each item gives two branches, take it or skip it, so n items give 2ⁿ leaves: 3 items, 8 leaves; 20 items, about a million.
One recursive function walks that tree: go(i, …) decides item i, calls go(i + 1, …) once per branch, and its base case is i == n, the end of the input, where one full set of choices is ready to use.

When the answer is built in a list, append the choice before the call and pop it after: one list is shared by every branch, and undoing the choice on the way back leaves it as it was for the next branch. A number passed as an argument needs no undo, since each call gets its own.
Cost: the nodes above the 2ⁿ leaves about double the count, so O(2ⁿ) calls, fine for n up to about 20. The recursion is n calls deep.

sum-of-all-subset-xor-totals: Each leaf here needs only one number, the XOR of the items taken. What would you pass down instead of a list, and what does the base case return?

blocks.say: Backtracking walks a decision tree: at each item I take it or skip it and recurse, undo the choice on the way back when I'm building a list, and stop at the end of the input, so n items give 2ⁿ leaves.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): list every 3-letter string of 0s and 1s with no two 1s next to each other.

The tree: each level picks the next letter, 0 or 1, so 2³ = 8 leaves. go(path): if len(path) == 3, save it; otherwise for c in "01", skip "1" when path ends in "1", else append c, call go(path), then pop.
Trace: 0, then 00, then 000 (saved) and 001 (saved). Pop back to 0, then 01, then 010 (saved); 011 is skipped.
Pop back to the empty path, then 1, then 10, then 100 and 101 (both saved). 11 is skipped, and with it the 2 leaves below it.
Answer: 5 strings. The pop after each call is what turns 00 back into 0 before 01 is tried; without it, path would keep growing.

first: Timer: 40 minutes. Stuck when it rings: one line in My notes on where, then take the help on its row one step at a time. Show the answer last and watch only the idea in its Video, then close it and code it from blank. Show the answer turns its bookmark on for you.
points: You solved next-greater questions with a monotonic stack of waiting indexes (Day 51) and Trapping Rain Water (Day 27). This hard asks for the area of the biggest rectangle that fits under a bar chart.

largest-rectangle-in-histogram: Step 1, brute force: try every pair of edges (i, j); the height is the shortest bar between them. How many pairs are there for 100,000 bars, and is that fast enough?
Step 2: turn it round. In the best rectangle, some bar is the shortest and sets the height. If bar i sets the height, how far can the rectangle stretch left and right, and what stops it?

Step 3: the worked example (the next step) finds the nearest taller building on both sides in one pass. Which comparison do you flip to get the nearest shorter bar instead? Once you have both, what are the width and the area for bar i? What about two bars of equal height?

Step 4: bars still on the stack at the end never met a shorter bar on the right: where does their rectangle end? A bar of height 0 added at the end is one way to finish them. Trace [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3] on paper: the answer is 10.

blocks.say: Each bar can be the shortest of its rectangle, which stretches until a shorter bar on each side; a stack of rising heights finds both in one pass, since the bar that pops bar i is its right limit and the bar left beneath it is its left limit, so the width is right − left − 1, and a final height-0 bar flushes the rest: O(n).
example: Practice problem (not NeetCode 250): buildings of heights [3, 1, 2, 5, 4] stand in a row, all different. For each, find the nearest taller building on its left and on its right.
Keep a stack of indexes whose heights fall from bottom to top: each is still waiting for a taller building on its right. Push 0 (3), then 1 (1).

Index 2 (height 2) is taller than index 1, so pop 1: its right answer is 2, and the index now beneath it, 0 (height 3), is its left answer. Whatever sits under a waiting building is taller than it and nearer than anything further down. Push 2.
Index 3 (height 5) pops 2 (right 3, left 0), then pops 0 (right 3, nothing beneath, so no taller building on its left). Push 3, then push 4 (height 4).

End: 3 and 4 are still waiting, so neither has a taller building on its right, and 4's left answer is 3, the one beneath it. Left [none, 0, 0, none, 3], right [3, 2, 3, none, none]: one pass, each index pushed and popped once, O(n).

blocks.title: Design a news feed: posts, fan-out, celebrities and a cursor
blocks.builds_on: Day 67 · fan-out on write vs on read, and the celebrity problem, Day 62 · a notification system's queues and workers, Day 25 · Snowflake IDs that sort by time, Day 41 · sharding and hot keys, Day 18 · cursor pagination, Day 13 · caching, Day 39 · message queues, and Day 32 · the 45-minute design framework
points: The ask: users follow others, post, and open a home feed of the posts of people they follow, newest first, and scroll through it. Ranking by a model, ads and comments are out of scope. Today's guide lab (optional) is SDS 0007's.

Requirements with numbers: 200 million daily users who open the feed 10 times a day and post about once in 10 days, each with about 200 followers. A feed loads in under 200 ms at p99, and a new post may take a few seconds to reach followers.

Estimates (Day 11): 2 billion feed reads a day is about 23,000 a second (69,000 at a 3× peak), but only about 230 posts a second. Reads win by about 100 to 1, so do the work at write time and make reads cheap.

Posts: a posts table sharded by author (Day 41), each with a Snowflake ID (Day 25), so sorting by ID sorts by time. Follows: (follower, followee) pairs, kept both ways so "who follows Asha" and "whom does Ravi follow" are each one lookup.

Fan-out on write (Day 67): a new post goes on a queue (Day 39), and workers add its ID to each follower's feed list in Redis (Day 13), trimmed to the newest 500 IDs. Reading a feed is one list read plus one batch fetch of the posts from a post cache. Lists hold IDs, not posts, so an edit or a delete shows everywhere.

Celebrities: 20 million posts a day × 200 followers is 4 billion feed writes, about 46,000 a second. One post by an account with 50 million followers is 50 million writes, about 18 minutes of that whole flow. So accounts above a threshold (say 100,000 followers) are not fanned out; their recent posts are pulled at read time and merged in (the hybrid).

Paging (Day 18): each response carries next_cursor, the oldest post ID shown, and the next request asks for IDs below it. New posts don't shift the pages, and a deleted post is just skipped when its ID is looked up.

Wrap up with what to watch: fan-out lag (seconds from post to feeds), the queue's backlog, feed p99, and memory: 500 IDs of 8 bytes for 200 million users is 800 GB of feed lists, so keep lists only for users active in the last month and rebuild the rest on login.
blocks.say: I store posts sharded by author with time-sorted Snowflake IDs, fan each new post's ID out on write to followers' feed lists in Redis through a queue, pull celebrities' posts at read time and merge them in, and page with a cursor of the last ID shown.
example: Asha has 300 followers and posts at 9:00 IST. The post service takes a Snowflake ID, writes the post to its author's shard and to the post cache, and puts {post ID, author} on the fan-out queue.
A fan-out worker reads Asha's 300 follower IDs and adds the post ID to the front of each one's feed list in Redis: 300 small writes, each list trimmed to 500.
A cricketer with 30 million followers posts a minute later. He is above the threshold, so nothing is fanned out; the post only goes on his own list of recent posts.

Ravi follows both and opens the app. The feed service reads his first 20 IDs, adds the cricketer's latest IDs, sorts them newest first, keeps 20, fetches those posts from the post cache in one batch, and returns them with next_cursor, the oldest ID shown.
Ravi scrolls: GET /v1/feed?cursor=<that ID> returns the 20 IDs below it. Five new posts arrived in the meantime, but they sit above the cursor, so this page neither repeats nor skips anything.

selftest.q: How many leaves does the take-or-skip tree have for 10 items, and where is its base case?
selftest.a: 2¹⁰ = 1,024 leaves. The base case is the end of the input, i == n, where one full set of choices is ready.

selftest.q: What is the Sum of All Subsets XOR Total of [1, 3]?
selftest.a: The subsets are [], [1], [3] and [1, 3], with XORs 0, 1, 3 and 1 ^ 3 = 2, so 6.

selftest.q: In Largest Rectangle in Histogram, a bar is popped from the stack by a shorter bar. What are the edges of the rectangle it sets the height of?
selftest.a: The bar that popped it is the first shorter bar on the right, and the bar left beneath it on the stack is the first shorter one on the left, so the width is right − left − 1. For [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3] the best is 5 × 2 = 10.

selftest.q: Why not fan out a celebrity's post on write?
selftest.a: 50 million followers means 50 million feed-list writes for one post, about 18 minutes of a system's whole fan-out at 46,000 writes a second. Their recent posts are pulled at read time and merged in instead.

selftest.q: Day 50: a stack-of-survivors loop has a while loop inside a for loop. Why is it still O(n)?
selftest.a: Each item is pushed once and popped at most once, so all the while loop's pops add up to at most n over the whole pass.

blocks.title: Backtracking: Subsets
blocks.builds_on: Day 69 · Backtracking
points: Yesterday each leaf needed one number. When the answer is the list of choices itself, keep one list, path, for the choices made so far: append before going down a branch, pop after coming back, so path is as it was for the next branch.
At a leaf, save a copy, `result.append(path[:])`. Saving path itself saves a reference to the one shared list, which the pops empty again, so every saved answer comes out the same: empty.
Cost: 2ⁿ leaves, each copied in up to n steps: O(n · 2ⁿ). That is also the size of the output, so nothing can do better. The recursion is n calls deep.
Test on an empty input (one answer, the empty list) and on one item (two answers).

subsets: Every answer is one leaf of yesterday's take-or-skip tree. What does a leaf add to the result here, and where do the append and the pop go around the take branch?

blocks.say: Subsets is the take-or-skip tree with a shared path: append, recurse, pop, and save a copy of the path at each leaf, O(n · 2ⁿ), which is the size of the answer.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): list every way to write "a1b" with each letter in lower or upper case.
go(i): when i == len(s), save "".join(path), a new string and so already a copy. A digit gives one branch; a letter gives two, lower and upper.
Trace: path a, then a 1, then a 1 b: save "a1b". Pop b and push B: save "a1B". Pop back to the empty path, push A, and the same again: "A1b", "A1B".
2 letters give 2² = 4 strings. A string of n letters gives 2ⁿ, each built in n steps: O(n · 2ⁿ), the size of the answer.

blocks.title: Trees (hard): Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
blocks.builds_on: Days 54 to 66 · Trees, and Day 5 · recursion and the call stack
first: Timer: 40 minutes. Stuck when it rings: one line in My notes on where, then take the help on its row one step at a time. Show the answer last and watch only the idea in its Video, then close it and code it from blank. Show the answer turns its bookmark on for you.
points: You found a tree's diameter on Day 58, where the helper returns one thing to the parent and records the real answer aside. This hard does the same with values that can be negative, and asks for the largest sum along any path.

binary-tree-maximum-path-sum: Step 1: every path has one highest node, where it bends (or ends). With that node fixed, the path is the node plus a route down into its left subtree and one down into its right. If you worked out those routes from scratch at every node, what would it cost on a tree shaped like a line?

Step 2: the worked example (the next step) finds the best route down from every node in one pass. A parent can extend only a route that goes straight down through one child, never one that already bends. So what should your helper record at each node, and what should it return?
Step 3: a subtree's best route can be negative. Should the path bending at a node ever include it?
Step 4: what should the record start at if every value in the tree is negative? Trace a single node −3 (answer −3), then [−10, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7] (answer 42).

blocks.say: The path bends at one top node, so at each node I record node + max(0, left gain) + max(0, right gain), but return node + max(0, left gain, right gain), because a parent can extend only one arm; the record starts at −∞ so an all-negative tree still gives its biggest node, in one O(n) pass.
example: Practice problem (not NeetCode 250): a delivery route as a tree, each stop worth tips minus fuel. Find the best total along a path that starts at the root and goes down, stopping at any node. Root 4; left −2 with children 5 and −6; right 1 with a right child −3.
best_down(node) = node.val + the largest of 0, best_down(left) and best_down(right). A branch whose best is negative counts as 0, because you can stop before it. best_down(None) = 0.
Leaves: 5 gives 5, −6 gives −6 and −3 gives −3. Node −2: −2 + max(0, 5, −6) = 3. Node 1: 1 + max(0, −3) = 1.
Root: 4 + max(0, 3, 1) = 7, the path 4 → −2 → 5. Passing through a negative node can pay, and stopping early (before −6 and −3) can too.
One post-order pass, O(n): each node returned the best route that starts at it and goes down.

blocks.title: Machine coding: an elevator system with states, requests and a dispatch strategy
blocks.builds_on: Day 37 · the State pattern, Day 65 · Command: actions as objects, Day 16 · Strategy, Day 63 · the coffee machine, the last machine-coding round, Day 21 · the machine-coding playbook and enums, and Day 30 · Observer
points: A 90-minute machine-coding round, like Day 63's coffee machine: 10 minutes for requirements, entities and states, then build in slices that run, then tests and a demo.

Requirements: one building, floors 0 to 9, two or more cars. A hall call is a floor and a direction (someone on floor 3 pressed up); a car call is a floor pressed inside one car. Out of scope: weight limits, emergencies, door sensors.

Run it as a tick-driven simulation: each tick, a car moves one floor or keeps its doors open. A car starts moving on the tick it is given a call, and opening its doors takes a tick of its own after it arrives. No threads and no sleeps, so a test can run 20 ticks and check where every car is.
Each car is Day 37's State pattern: Idle, MovingUp, MovingDown and DoorsOpen, each with a tick(car) that does one step and picks the next state. A Direction enum (Day 21) holds UP and DOWN.

Each button press becomes a request object, HallCall or CarCall, that the controller queues and runs on the next tick (Day 65's Command): requests can then be logged, replayed in a test, or cancelled.

Which car takes a hall call is a Strategy (Day 16). The simplest good one: the nearest car that is idle or already heading to that floor in the same direction. Zoning (car A serves floors 0 to 4) is a second strategy, swapped in without touching the cars.

How a car orders its stops: it keeps going one way, serving every stop on the way, and turns only when nothing is left ahead. SCAN, the classic elevator algorithm, runs to the last floor before turning; LOOK turns (or goes idle) at the last request, which is what real lifts do.
Extensions to discuss: a floor display that subscribes to car moves (Day 30), a peak-hour strategy that parks idle cars at the ground floor, and a maintenance state that takes a car out of dispatch.
blocks.say: I run the lifts as a tick-driven simulation: each car is a state machine (Idle, MovingUp, MovingDown, DoorsOpen), every button press is a request object the controller queues, a swappable strategy picks the car for a hall call, and each car serves its stops LOOK-style, turning at the last request.
example: Floors 0 to 9; car A idle at floor 0, car B idle at floor 7. One tick moves a car one floor or keeps its doors open.

Tick 1: a hall call at floor 3, going up. The strategy picks the nearest car that is idle or heading there the same way: A is 3 floors away and B 4, so A takes it, with stops {3}, and becomes MovingUp. A reaches 3 at tick 3 and opens its doors at tick 4.
Tick 3: a hall call at floor 5, going down. A is on its way up, the wrong direction for a down call, so B (idle, 2 floors away) takes it, reaches 5 at tick 4 and opens at tick 5.

Tick 6: the rider in A presses 8, a car call that only A can serve. A climbs from 3 and opens at 8 at tick 11; nothing is left in either direction, so it goes Idle there. LOOK stops at the last request; SCAN would have gone on to floor 9 first.
Each press was a request object queued with the controller, each car's step came from its state, and the choice of car came from a strategy that a test can swap.

About 20 minutes of tests that replay the worked example: after tick 4, A's doors are open at floor 3; after tick 5, B's doors are open at 5; after tick 11, A's doors are open at 8, and on tick 12 it is Idle at 8. Then one more: a car going up past floor 5 doesn't stop for a down call there.

blocks.title: Pre-training: the data, the objective and scaling laws
blocks.builds_on: Day 49 · a neural language model trained to predict the next character, Day 45 · the average −log p loss, where guessing evenly over 27 characters gives ln 27 ≈ 3.30, Day 8 · cross-entropy, Day 66 · tokenisation with BPE, and Day 59 · the transformer block
points: Pre-training is Day 49's job at full size: predict the next token, at every position at once (Day 57's mask), over trillions of tokens of text. Nothing is labelled by hand; the text itself is the answer key.

The loss is cross-entropy over the whole vocabulary: with the true token as a one-hot vector y and the model's probabilities p, loss = −Σ y_c log p_c, which is just −log p(true token), averaged over every position. It is Day 8's loss with tens of thousands of classes instead of 2.

Perplexity = e^loss: how many equally likely tokens the model is torn between. Day 45's even guess over 27 characters has loss ln 27 ≈ 3.30 and perplexity 27; a loss of 3.0 is a perplexity of about 20.

The data: web crawls (Common Crawl), books, code and Wikipedia, cleaned before training: keep the wanted languages, drop spam, boilerplate and personal data, and remove duplicates, exact and near (repeated text gets memorised and wastes compute). Today's guide lesson covers that pipeline, so the block's own reading is shorter.

Training compute is about 6 × N × D floating-point operations (FLOPs), for N parameters and D tokens: about 2 per parameter per token going forward and 4 going back (Day 38). Llama 2 7B: 6 × 7 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10¹² ≈ 8.4 × 10²² FLOPs; Meta reported 184,320 GPU-hours, so the GPUs ran at about 40% of their peak.

Scaling laws: the loss falls smoothly and predictably as N, D and compute grow, so a small run predicts a big one. Chinchilla (2022) found that for a fixed compute budget, parameters and tokens should grow together, about 20 tokens per parameter: its 70B model on 1.4 trillion tokens beat 280B Gopher, trained on 300 billion.

Models today train far past 20 tokens per parameter on purpose: Llama 2 7B saw 2 trillion tokens, about 14 times Chinchilla's 140 billion. Training costs more, but a smaller model is cheaper every time it answers, and a deployed model answers billions of times.
In an interview: the objective (next-token cross-entropy), the data and its cleaning, the compute (6ND), and the trade-off between a bigger model and more tokens.
blocks.say: Pre-training minimises next-token cross-entropy over trillions of cleaned, deduplicated tokens; compute is about 6 × parameters × tokens, Chinchilla says about 20 tokens per parameter for a fixed budget, and today's models train smaller and longer because inference cost depends on size.
example: A model predicts the next token over a 4-token vocabulary at two positions: [0.7, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1] where the true token is token 0, and [0.2, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1] where it is token 2.
With one-hot labels only the true token's probability counts: −ln 0.7 = 0.357 and −ln 0.2 = 1.609.
Average loss (0.357 + 1.609) ÷ 2 = 0.983, so the perplexity is e^0.983 ≈ 2.67: on average as unsure as choosing between under three tokens.
Scale it up: a 1-billion-parameter model, Chinchilla-style, wants about 20 × 10⁹ = 20 billion tokens, and 6 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10¹⁰ = 1.2 × 10²⁰ FLOPs of training.

tasks.text: About 5 minutes in Python (`uv run python`, `import math`): GPT-2's vocabulary has 50,257 tokens. What loss does an even guess over it give, and what perplexity? (ln 50,257 ≈ 10.82, perplexity 50,257.) What perplexity does a loss of 3.0 give? (e³ ≈ 20.1.)

About 5 minutes: work out 6 × N × D for Llama 2 7B (N = 7 × 10⁹, D = 2 × 10¹²): 8.4 × 10²² FLOPs. An A100 GPU peaks at 312 × 10¹² FLOPs a second; at 40% of that, how many GPU-hours is it? (About 187,000, close to the 184,320 Meta reported.) How many tokens would Chinchilla's rule give a 7B model? (140 billion.)

Code it on Deep-ML: #134 Compute Multi-class Cross-Entropy Loss. Today's loss for a batch of rows: first clip the probabilities with `np.clip(predicted_probs, epsilon, 1 - epsilon)`, because the first test has probabilities of exactly 0, and 0 × log 0 is 0 × −∞, which numpy turns into nan. The labels are one-hot, so `-(true_labels * np.log(p)).sum(axis=1)` is each row's loss; return the mean over the rows as a float. It runs in the browser and numpy is fine. selftest.q: In Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum, what does the helper return and what does it record?

selftest.q: SCAN or LOOK: what is the difference for an elevator?
selftest.a: Both keep going one way and serve every stop on the way. SCAN runs to the last floor before turning; LOOK turns, or goes idle, at the last request.

selftest.q: A model's loss is 3.0 per token. What is its perplexity, and how many tokens would Chinchilla's rule give a 1-billion-parameter model?

selftest.q: Day 52: why are attention scores divided by √d before the softmax?
selftest.a: Dot products of long vectors are large, and large scores make softmax put almost all the weight on one token, which leaves tiny gradients. Dividing by √d keeps the scores in a range where the weights stay spread and training works.

blocks.title: Backtracking: Combination Sum and Combination Sum II
blocks.builds_on: Days 69 and 70 · Backtracking
points: When the order of the choices doesn't matter, [a, b] and [b, a] are one answer. Pass a start index: each call chooses only from the items at that index or later, so every answer is built in one order and found once.
Reuse or once: if an item may be chosen again, the next call keeps the same start index; if each item may be used once, the next call starts one past it.
Stop a branch as soon as it can't succeed. With the items sorted, once one is too big for what is left, every later one is too, so break out of the loop rather than continue.

combination-target-sum: Draw the tree for candidates [2, 3] and target 7 by hand. At each node, which candidates may come next so that [2, 2, 3] is built once, and not again as [2, 3, 2] and [3, 2, 2]? What is the base case, and when does a branch give up?
combination-target-sum-ii: Here each number is used at most once, and the input can hold equal numbers: [1, 1, 2] with target 3 would give [1, 2] twice. After sorting, where do the equal numbers sit?
Two equal numbers tried at the same depth start the same subtree. Which one should the loop skip, and why is taking both of them at different depths still fine?

blocks.say: For combinations I pass a start index so each set is built in one order: the same index when an item can repeat, the next one when it is used once; I sort, break once a candidate is bigger than what is left, and skip a number equal to the one before it at the same depth, so equal inputs don't give equal answers.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): an ice-cream shop has chocolate, mango and vanilla (C, M, V). List every cup of 3 scoops, where the order in the cup doesn't matter and a flavour may repeat.
Without a start index, each of the 3 levels picks any flavour: 3³ = 27 ordered lists, and CMV, MCV, VMC and the rest are one cup counted 6 times.
go(start, cup): when len(cup) == 3, save a copy. Otherwise, for i from start to 2, append flavour i, call go(i, cup), since the same flavour may come again, then pop.
Trace: CCC, CCM, CCV, then back up to C: CMM, CMV, CVV. Then from M: MMM, MMV, MVV. Then VVV. 10 cups, each built once, because a later level never picks a flavour earlier in the list.
Count check before coding: 3 scoops from 3 flavours with repeats is C(3 + 3 − 1, 3) = C(5, 3) = 10, the number of multisets, which the primary explains.
