blocks.title: Sampling: temperature, top-k, top-p and beam search
blocks.builds_on: Day 64 · a tiny GPT's generate loop, with temperature and top_k, Day 36 · softmax, and Day 45 · sampling the next token with torch.multinomial
points: A model's last layer gives logits, one score per token in the vocabulary; softmax (Day 36) turns them into probabilities. Decoding is how you pick the next token from them, one token at a time.
Greedy: always take the most likely token. It is fast and gives the same answer every time, but it tends to repeat itself and misses a better sentence that starts with a less likely word.
Temperature T: divide the logits by T before softmax. T below 1 sharpens the distribution (the top token gains), T above 1 flattens it (rare tokens gain), and T near 0 becomes greedy.
Top-k: keep the k most likely tokens, drop the rest, and renormalise so they add up to 1. A fixed k keeps too many tokens when the model is sure and too few when it isn't.
Top-p (nucleus sampling): sort by probability and keep the smallest set whose total reaches p, say 0.9, then renormalise. The set grows when the model is unsure and shrinks when it is sure.

The order, as in Day 64's generate: logits ÷ T, then the top-k or top-p cut, then softmax, then draw one token. Use a low temperature (or 0) where there is one right answer, such as extracting fields or writing code, and a higher one for open-ended writing.

Beam search: keep the B most likely partial sequences, extend each by every token, and keep the best B again by total probability (in practice the sum of log-probabilities). It suits tasks with one right answer, such as translation; for open-ended chat its text comes out dull and repetitive.
blocks.say: Decoding turns logits into the next token: greedy takes the top one, temperature divides the logits to sharpen or flatten them, top-k and top-p cut to the likely tokens before sampling, with top-p adapting to how sure the model is, and beam search keeps the B best partial sequences for tasks with one right answer.
example: A model's next-token logits are [2, 1, 0] for chai, coffee and lassi.

T = 1: softmax gives [0.665, 0.245, 0.090]. T = 0.5 doubles the logits to [4, 2, 0]: [0.867, 0.117, 0.016], chai nearly every time. T = 2 halves them to [1, 0.5, 0]: [0.506, 0.307, 0.186], much flatter.
Top-k with k = 2 at T = 1: drop lassi and divide 0.665 and 0.245 by their sum, 0.910: [0.731, 0.269, 0].

Top-p with p = 0.9: sorted, chai alone is 0.665 and chai plus coffee is 0.910, which reaches 0.9, so both stay, the same as top-k 2 here. With p = 0.6, chai alone already reaches it, so the draw is greedy.

points: When order matters, [1, 2] and [2, 1] are different answers, so a start index would lose some: every level may choose any item not used yet. Keep a used marker per item (a list of booleans or a set): mark before going down, unmark after coming back, like append and pop.

Say the count before coding, since it is the size of the answer and sets the cost: n items in order give n! answers (3! = 6, 8! = 40,320); k of n where order doesn't matter give C(n, k) = n! ÷ (k! (n − k)!), so C(4, 2) = 6.
Prune a branch that can't be completed: if fewer items are left than places to fill, return before going further.

blocks.say: When order doesn't matter I pass a start index, C(n, k) answers; when it does, every level tries each unused item, marking it used before the call and unmarking after, n! answers, so the cost is about n! × n to copy them out.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): put the numbers 1 to 3 in positions 1 to 3 so that at every position, the number divides the position or the position divides the number. List the arrangements.
go(pos): when pos is 4, save a copy. Otherwise, for each unused number that fits position pos: mark it used, append it, call go(pos + 1), then pop and unmark.
Start with 1: position 2 can take 2 but not 3 (neither divides the other), then 3 fits position 3: [1, 2, 3]. Start with 2: position 2 takes 1, then 3: [2, 1, 3].
Start with 3: position 2 takes 1 or 2. 3, 1 leaves 2 for position 3, which fails, so that branch dies; 3, 2 leaves 1, which divides 3: [3, 2, 1].
3 of the 3! = 6 orders survive. Unmarking on the way back is what lets 2 be tried at position 1 after the branch that used it at position 2.

blocks.title: Chain of responsibility: pass a request along handlers
blocks.builds_on: Day 51 · Decorator: wrap an object to add a step, Day 16 · Strategy, Day 48 · a rate limiter, and Day 18 · API design and status codes
points: Chain of responsibility: a request passes along a line of handlers. Each one either handles it, and the chain stops, or passes it to the next. The sender only knows the first handler.

An API pipeline: a per-IP rate limit, then auth, then a per-user rate limit (Day 48), then validation, then the handler. Too many requests from one IP get 429; a missing token gets 401; too many from one user get 429; a bad body gets 400; only a good request reaches the handler.

Each handler holds a link to the next and has one method, handle(request). A base class does the passing, `return self.next.handle(request) if self.next else default`, so each concrete handler writes only its own check.

The order is a decision. A cheap per-IP limit goes first, so a flood of failed logins is stopped before auth spends work on it; the per-user limit goes after auth, because it needs to know the user; and auth goes before validation, so a caller you don't know learns nothing about your rules from a 400.

Versus Decorator (Day 51): both put a line of objects around a call, but a decorator always passes on and adds behaviour, while a chain handler may stop the request. Versus Strategy (Day 16): a strategy is one algorithm chosen up front; a chain tries several in turn.
You have used it already: web framework middleware, such as Django's, is a chain around every request.
The risk: a request that falls off the end unhandled. Give the end of the chain a default answer, such as 404.
blocks.say: Chain of responsibility passes a request along handlers that each handle it or pass it on, like auth, rate limit and validation middleware in front of an API; adding a step is one new handler and one changed link, and unlike a decorator, a handler may stop the request.
example: A food-delivery app's support chain: a help bot answers "where is my order?", an agent approves refunds up to ₹500, and a manager handles anything bigger. Every ticket goes to the bot first.
"Where is my order?": the bot matches it and answers. The chain stops at the first handler.
"Refund ₹300": the bot can't, so it passes it to the agent, who can (300 ≤ 500) and approves it.
"Refund ₹2,000": the bot passes it on, the agent passes it on (over ₹500), and the manager handles it.
Adding a fraud check before the agent is one new handler and one changed link. No other handler changes, and the app still sends every ticket to the bot.

blocks.builds_on: Days 69 to 72 · Backtracking
points: When the input holds equal values, two branches can build the same answer: [1, 2, 2] has 8 subsets by position but only 6 different ones.

One fix: sort so equal values sit together, then within one loop of one call try each value once, skipping an item equal to the one before it in that loop (Day 71). Equal values can still be chosen together at different depths.
Another fix: count each value with collections.Counter and branch over the distinct values, taking one off its count before the call and putting it back after.

subsets-ii: Subsets II: with [1, 2, 2] sorted, which two branches of Day 70's take-or-skip tree build the same [1, 2]? If you skip one 2, what should happen to the 2s after it?
permutations-ii: Permutations II: [1, 1, 2] has 3! = 6 orders but only 3 different ones. At one position, what makes two choices the same, and which of today's two fixes fits best?

blocks.say: With equal values in the input I either sort and skip a value equal to the one before it in the same loop, or branch over a Counter of the distinct values, taking one off before the call and putting it back after, so every answer is built once.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): you have letter tiles A, A and B. How many different non-empty strings can you make, using each tile at most once?
Counter {A: 2, B: 1}. go(): for each letter whose count is above 0, count one new string, take one off its count, call go(), then put it back.
Trace: A (1). From A: A gives AA (2), then B gives AAB (3); B gives AB (4), then A gives ABA (5). Back at the top: B (6), then BA (7), then BAA (8).
8 strings, each built once, because each level branches over the distinct letters, not the tiles: the first A and the second A are one branch, not two.
Branching over the 3 tiles instead would build 15 strings by position (3 + 6 + 6), with repeats to remove.

blocks.title: Inference: prefill, decode and the KV cache
blocks.builds_on: Day 64 · a tiny GPT's generate loop, Day 57 · self-attention with queries, keys and values, and the causal mask, Day 59 · the transformer block, and Day 71 · sampling
points: A model answers in two phases. Prefill: the whole prompt goes through at once, every position in parallel, which keeps the GPU busy with big matrix multiplies. Decode: then one new token at a time, each a full pass through every layer.

With the causal mask (Day 57), a token's key and value depend only on itself and the tokens before it, so they never change once computed. Recomputing them at every step, as Day 64's generate does, is wasted work.

The KV cache keeps each layer's K and V for every token so far. A decode step computes q, k and v for the new token only, appends its k and v, and scores q against the cached keys: the work per step grows with the length, not with its square.

Memory per token = 2 (K and V) × layers × model width d × bytes per number. Llama 2 7B: 2 × 32 × 4,096 × 2 bytes (fp16) = 524,288 bytes, 0.5 MiB per token. Today's guide lesson covers this arithmetic, so the block's own reading is shorter.

A 4,096-token context is then 2 GiB per sequence, and 16 sequences at once need 32 GiB, more than the model's weights (about 13.5 GB). So the cache, not the weights, often limits how many users a GPU serves at once.

Shrinking it: grouped-query attention (GQA) shares each K and V head among several query heads. Llama 3 8B keeps 8 KV heads of 128 numbers instead of 32: 128 KiB per token, a quarter. Storing the cache in 8 bits halves it again.

Two numbers to watch: time to first token (TTFT), set by prefill and the prompt's length, and time per output token (TPOT), set by decode, which is limited by reading the weights and the cache from memory, not by arithmetic.
blocks.say: Inference is a parallel prefill over the prompt, which sets time to first token, then one decode step per token, which sets time per output token; the KV cache stores each layer's keys and values so a step only computes the new token's, at a memory cost of 2 × layers × d × bytes per token, 0.5 MiB for a 7B model, which GQA cuts.
example: Llama 2 7B (32 layers, width 4,096, fp16) answers a 1,000-token prompt with 200 tokens.
Prefill: all 1,000 prompt tokens go through in one pass, and each layer stores their keys and values: 1,000 × 524,288 bytes = 500 MiB of cache.
Decode, first step: each layer computes q, k and v for the new token only, scores its q against 1,001 keys (1,000 cached plus its own), and adds 0.5 MiB to the cache.
After 200 tokens the cache is 1,200 × 0.5 MiB = 600 MiB for this one request. Without it, every step would redo the keys and values of all the tokens before it, at every layer.
16 users at the full 4,096 tokens: 16 × 2 GiB = 32 GiB of cache beside about 13.5 GB of weights, so memory caps how many requests share a GPU.

blocks.builds_on: Days 69 to 73 · Backtracking, and Day 6 · trees and graphs
points: Prune early: check a partial answer as you build it, and return the moment it can't lead to a valid one. Building everything and filtering at the end pays for the whole tree.

On a grid, the choices at each cell are its 4 neighbours, and a path may not use a cell twice. Mark a cell when you step on it and unmark it on the way back, so other paths can still use it: Day 6's visited set, undone like append and pop.
Marking in place, by setting the cell to '#' and putting its letter back after, saves a separate set; put it back on every way out of the call.
Cost of a grid search for a path of length L: from each of the m × n cells, at most 4 choices at the first step and 3 after, O(m × n × 3^L).

generate-parentheses: Generate Parentheses: of the 2^(2n) strings of brackets, most are invalid. At each step, what must be true for '(' to be allowed, and what for ')'?
search-for-word: Word Search: what are the base cases of the search from one cell, in what order do you check them, and where do the mark and the unmark go?

blocks.say: I prune as I build, adding only what can still lead to a valid answer, and on a grid I mark a cell before exploring its neighbours and unmark it on the way back so other paths can use it: O(m × n × 3^L) for a word of length L.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): a gold mine is a grid where 0 is empty. Start at any cell with gold, move up, down, left or right, never step on a 0 or on a cell twice, and collect the most gold. Grid [[0, 6, 0], [5, 8, 7], [0, 9, 0]].
dfs(r, c): outside the grid or on a 0, return 0. Otherwise keep g = grid[r][c], set the cell to 0 (marked), take g plus the best dfs of its 4 neighbours, then put g back (unmarked) and return that.
From 9: mark it and go up to 8. From 8, each of 6, 5 and 7 is a dead end, since its other neighbours are 0, so 8 adds at most 8 + 7 = 15, and 9 gives 9 + 15 = 24.
Without the unmark, 8 would still be 0 when the search later starts from 7, and 7 would stop at 7. Putting g back lets every start see the whole grid.
Try every gold cell as a start and keep the best: 24, from 9 or from 7.

blocks.title: Blob storage and CDNs: files, presigned URLs and edge caching
blocks.builds_on: Day 4 · a request's journey: DNS, TCP and HTTP, Day 13 · caching with TTLs and hit rates, Day 20 · choosing a database, and Day 11 · estimates
points: Photos, videos and PDFs are blobs: large bytes nobody searches inside. Keep the bytes in object storage (Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage), the metadata (owner, size, type, status) in a database (Day 20), and in your rows only the object's key.

Object storage is a flat store of key → bytes over HTTP: very durable (copies across machines and data centres), cheap per GB, and slower per request than a database. An object is replaced whole, never edited in place.

Presigned URL: the app server signs a URL that lets one client upload (PUT) or download (GET) one key until an expiry time. The bytes go straight between the phone and storage, never through your servers. On S3 a presigned URL lasts at most 7 days.

Multipart upload: split a big file into parts (S3 allows up to 10,000, numbered 1 to 10,000), upload them in parallel, retry only a part that fails, then one last call joins them. S3 suggests it from about 100 MB.

A CDN keeps copies of popular files on edge servers near users, in Mumbai, Delhi or Chennai, so a request travels a short way and the origin sees only the misses. Each copy lives for its TTL (Day 13), set by the Cache-Control header.

Pull CDN: the edge fetches a file from the origin on its first miss, then keeps it; simple, and right for most traffic. Push CDN: you upload files to the CDN ahead of time; for big files that rarely change, or a planned launch.
Changing a cached file: don't wait for TTLs or purge every edge. Put a version or a content hash in the name (logo.3f9a.png) with a long TTL; a new version is a new URL, so nobody gets a stale copy.
Private files through a CDN use signed URLs too, checked at the edge, so a shared link works only until it expires.
blocks.say: I keep file bytes in object storage and only their key and metadata in the database, let clients upload and download straight to storage with short-lived presigned URLs, using multipart for big files, and serve reads through a CDN with long TTLs on versioned URLs, so a change is a new URL rather than a purge.
example: A restaurant owner on a food-delivery app uploads a 1 GB kitchen video. The API writes a metadata row (status uploading, key videos/r42/9f1c.mp4) and starts a multipart upload.
The API returns a presigned URL for each part: 1 GB in 10 MB parts is 100 parts. The phone uploads them straight to storage, a few at a time, and retries any part that fails.
The phone calls complete, storage joins the parts, and the API marks the row ready. No byte of the video passed through the app servers.
Reading: menu photos get 1 million views a day at 0.5 MB each, 500 GB a day. With 95% of requests served by the CDN, the origin sends only 25 GB.
The owner replaces a menu photo: it gets a new key with a new hash and the row points to it. The old cached copy is simply never asked for again.

first: Fridays start with revision, but today's guide reading (about 10 minutes) shares this block, so there are no re-solves today: anything due stays in the Revise row, and Sunday's review starts with it. That leaves a 20-minute timer for today's problem. Stuck when it rings, take the help on its row one step at a time, out of the 15 minutes Friday leaves spare.
points: Every backtracking problem so far had one skeleton: a path of the choices made so far, a loop over the choices allowed next, and a base case that records a copy of the path. The real work is naming the choice.

When the input is a sequence that must be used up in order, the choice can be how much of it the next piece takes. The recursion then carries the index where the rest starts, and the base case is that index reaching the end.
Check a choice before you recurse into it, not after: a piece that breaks the rule cuts off its whole branch for the price of one check.

palindrome-partitioning: Before coding, draw the top of the tree for "aab": what are the root's children, and which of them survive the rule?
Optional step up: the same piece gets checked again on many branches, at O(length) each with Day 20's two pointers. What could you work out once, before the search, so every check is O(1)?

blocks.say: I backtrack over where the next piece ends: from index i I try every end j, recurse from j + 1 only if s[i..j] is a palindrome, and record a copy of the path when i reaches the end; a string has up to 2^(n − 1) splits, so the worst case is O(n · 2^n).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): list every way to cut a 4-metre ribbon into pieces of 1 or 3 metres, in order. Day 7's ways(n) counted sums like these; today we list them.
State: the position reached so far and the path of pieces. Choices at each position: a 1 or a 3, if it doesn't run past 4. Base case: position 4, record a copy of the path.

From 0, take 1 four times: position 4, record [1, 1, 1, 1]. Undo to position 3: a 3 would reach 6, so that branch is cut before any call. Undo to 2: a 3 would reach 5, cut. Undo to 1: a 3 reaches 4, record [1, 3].
Undo to 0 and take a 3: position 3, then a 1 reaches 4, record [3, 1]. Three ways in all.
The fit check ran before each call, so a dead branch cost one comparison. The answers themselves can be exponential in number, so the time is at least the number of answers times their length.

blocks.title: Transactions and ACID: what keeps a transfer whole
blocks.builds_on: Day 20 · ACID named, indexes, and a transfer inside with conn: in sqlite3, Day 26 · race conditions and a mutex around a critical section, Day 46 · distributed transactions across services, and Day 54 · running SQL from Python with sqlite3
points: A transaction makes several statements one unit: BEGIN, the statements, then COMMIT to keep them all or ROLLBACK to undo them all. Day 20 named the four ACID properties; today is how a database keeps each one, and what breaks without it. (Day 46: across services no single transaction covers both sides; inside one database, always use one.)

Autocommit: with no BEGIN, each statement is its own transaction and is saved the moment it runs. A transfer is two UPDATEs, so a crash between them saves the debit without the credit, and the money is gone.

Atomicity, all or nothing even across a crash: the database writes each change to a log before it changes the data (a write-ahead log; SQLite's default is a rollback journal), so after a crash it can undo a half-done transaction.

Consistency: the rules you declare, such as NOT NULL, UNIQUE, foreign keys and CHECK (balance >= 0), hold after every transaction. A statement that breaks one fails, and rolling back keeps the whole transfer out. Rules the database can't see, such as "the total never changes", stay the app's job.

Isolation: transactions running at once don't see each other's half-done work; at its strongest, the result is as if they ran one after another. It is Day 26's mutex idea for data: databases use locks or keep old row versions, and offer weaker levels for speed (Day 82). SQLite simply allows one writer at a time.
Durability: COMMIT returns only once the log is safely on disk, so a power cut after it loses nothing.

Python's sqlite3: `with conn:` commits on success and rolls back on an exception (Day 20). `sqlite3.connect(..., isolation_level=None)` gives autocommit, and then you write BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK yourself. Today's guide reading (about 5 minutes) shares this block.
blocks.say: A transaction makes several statements one unit: atomic because a log lets the database undo a half-done change, consistent with the rules I declare, isolated with locks or row versions, and durable because COMMIT waits for the log to reach disk; without one, a transfer that crashes between its debit and its credit loses money.
example: accounts: Asha ₹500 and Ravi ₹100, total 600, with CHECK (balance >= 0). A transfer of ₹200 from Asha to Ravi is a debit, then a credit.
Autocommit, crash after the debit: Asha 300, Ravi 100, total 400. ₹200 has vanished, and nothing in the database knows.
BEGIN, debit, crash, ROLLBACK: the journal undoes the debit, so Asha 500, Ravi 100, total 600.

Ravi sends ₹1,000, credit first: inside a transaction the debit fails the CHECK and the rollback takes the credit away too, 500 and 100. In autocommit the credit stays: Asha 1,500, total 1,600, money created from nothing.
Commit a transfer to a database file, close it and reopen it: the change is there. An UPDATE made after it and never committed is gone.

tasks.text: In d75.py, open `conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:", isolation_level=None)`, which is autocommit, and run this with `conn.executescript(...)`, ready to paste: `CREATE TABLE accounts (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, balance INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (balance >= 0)); INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (1, 'Asha', 500), (2, 'Ravi', 100);` Write `transfer(conn, src, dst, amount, crash=False)`: debit src, `raise RuntimeError("power cut")` if crash, then credit dst. Send ₹200 from Asha to Ravi with crash=True, catch the error, and print the balances and `SELECT SUM(balance)`: Asha 300, Ravi 100, total 400.

Rebuild the table and run the same crash between `conn.execute("BEGIN")` and `conn.execute("COMMIT")`, with `conn.execute("ROLLBACK")` in the except: 500, 100, total 600. Then send ₹1,000 from Ravi to Asha, credit first, once inside a transaction and once in autocommit: the CHECK raises `sqlite3.IntegrityError` both times. Inside the transaction, catch it too and ROLLBACK: the failed UPDATE alone is undone, so until your ROLLBACK the credit is still there (Asha 1,500), and after it the balances are 500 and 100. Autocommit leaves Asha 1,500 and a total of 1,600. Say which ACID letter each run shows.

selftest.q: In Palindrome Partitioning, what is the choice at each step, and when do you record an answer?
selftest.a: Where the next piece ends: from index i, try every end j with s[i..j] a palindrome and recurse from j + 1. Record a copy of the path when i reaches the end of the string.

selftest.q: Ignoring the palindrome rule, how many ways can a string of length n be cut into pieces?
selftest.a: 2^(n − 1): each of the n − 1 gaps between letters is either cut or not.

selftest.q: A transfer debits Asha ₹200 and the app crashes before crediting Ravi. What happens in autocommit, and inside a transaction?
selftest.a: In autocommit the debit is already saved, so ₹200 vanishes. Inside a transaction the database rolls the debit back (atomicity) and both balances are as before.

selftest.q: What lets a committed transaction survive a power cut?
selftest.a: Durability: the database writes the change to a log on disk before COMMIT returns, so after a crash it can recover every committed change from the log.

selftest.q: Day 55: in a key-value store like Dynamo, what is hinted handoff?
selftest.a: When a replica is down, another node accepts its writes with a note saying whose they are, and hands them over when the replica comes back, so writes keep working through a short failure.

blocks.title: Backtracking: letters from a phone keypad
blocks.builds_on: Days 69 to 75 · Backtracking, and Day 2 · dicts
points: Some searches have no rule to break: every complete path is an answer. Backtracking is then simply a clean way to build every combination, and the work is counting them before you code.
Count first: the number of answers is the product of the number of choices at each level. Levels with 3, 3 and 4 choices give 36 answers, and building each one costs O(n).
Build the answer in a list and join it at the leaf. A string can't change, so `path + ch` copies the whole string on every call (Day 55's hard counted those copies).

combinations-of-a-phone-number: What does each level of the tree stand for, and where do that level's choices come from?
The input can be empty: should that return an empty list or a list holding one empty string? Check the problem's examples.

blocks.say: Each digit is one level of the tree and its letters are that level's choices, so I recurse digit by digit with a path, join the path at the end, and the answer count is the product of the letter counts, up to 4^n, each costing O(n) to build.
example: Practice problem (not NeetCode 250, LeetCode 320): list every abbreviation of "ab", where each letter is either kept or replaced by a count, and counts next to each other join into one number.
Count first: 2 choices per letter, so 2 × 2 = 4 answers. "word" would have 2⁴ = 16.
Carry the path and a running count of skipped letters. Keep a: write the count if there is one, then a. Keep b: record "ab". Back up and skip b instead: the count is 1, record "a1".
Back to the start and skip a: the count is 1. Keep b: write 1, then b, record "1b". Skip b too: the count is 2, record "2". Four answers, as counted.
Each answer takes O(n) to build, so the time is O(n · 2^n). Joining skipped letters needed one extra number in the state: the running count. Today's problem needs only the path.

blocks.title: Trees (hard): Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
blocks.builds_on: Days 54 and 55 · the three DFS orders and preorder with your own stack, Day 60 · visiting a tree level by level, Day 65 · rebuilding a tree, and Day 14 · packing a list of strings into one string
first: Timer: 40 minutes. Stuck when it rings: one line in My notes on where, then take the help on its row one step at a time. Show the answer last and watch only the idea in its Video, then close it and code it from blank. Show the answer turns its bookmark on for you.
points: You can walk a tree in every order (Days 54, 55 and 60) and rebuild one from two orders (Day 65). This hard asks for one string that holds a tree's whole shape, and a way to read it back.

serialize-and-deserialize-binary-tree: Step 1: write the preorder of two different small trees that give the same list of values. What did the trees have that the list lost?
Step 2: what could you write in the string where a child is missing, so that no two shapes give the same string? How many entries does a tree of n nodes then produce?

Step 3, reading it back: your reader takes the next entry. If it is a value, what must be read next for that node, and in what order? If it is your empty mark, what does it return? How do all the calls share one position in the list?

Step 4: values can be negative or have several digits, so how do the entries stay apart (Day 14)? Trace your two trees from Step 1 through both functions on paper, then try a level-order version (Day 60) if time is left.

blocks.say: I write the preorder with a marker such as N for every empty child, comma-separated, so n nodes give 2n + 1 entries and the shape is unambiguous; to read it back, a recursive function takes the next entry from one shared iterator, returns None for N, or builds the node and then its left and right subtrees: O(n) both ways.
example: Practice problem (not NeetCode 250): evaluate "* + 2 3 4", the prefix (Polish) form of (2 + 3) × 4, Day 54's expression tree written in preorder, reading the tokens left to right only once.
Write read(): take the next token. A number is a leaf, so return it. An operator always has two operands: call read() for the left one, then read() for the right one, and combine them.
read() takes "*" and needs two operands. Its first read() takes "+", whose own two reads take 2 and 3, giving 5. Its second read() takes 4. Result 5 × 4 = 20.
Every call takes tokens from one shared place: `it = iter(tokens)` before the first call and `next(it)` inside read(), so no call needs to know where its operand ends. Each token is read once: O(n).
Prefix alone is enough here because each token says how many operands follow it: two after an operator, none after a number.

blocks.title: Design a chat app like WhatsApp: connections, delivery, ticks and groups
blocks.builds_on: Day 60 · WebSockets and pub/sub to whichever server holds a connection, Day 41 · partition keys and sharding, Day 53 · LSM trees for heavy writes, Day 25 · ids ordered by time, Day 62 · notifications and push, Day 67 · fan-out on write vs on read, Day 74 · blob storage, presigned URLs and CDNs, and Day 32 · the 45-minute design framework
points: The ask: 1:1 and group chats (up to about 100 members), messages in order within a chat, sent, delivered and read ticks, messages kept for offline users (say up to 30 days), photos, and one user on several devices. Start with Day 32's framework and numbers.

Connections: each online phone keeps one WebSocket (Day 60) to a connection server. Those servers hold state, so something must say where a user is: each server subscribes to the channels of the users it holds, and whoever sends publishes to the receiver's channel.
Message flow: the chat service gives the message the next sequence number in its chat, saves it, and only then delivers it. Save first, so a crash can't lose a message the sender already saw as sent.

Storage: messages keyed by chat id and sorted by sequence number, so one chat sits on one shard (Day 41) and "messages after 117" is one range read. Heavy writes suit an LSM-based wide-column store (Day 53). Order only has to hold within a chat, so a counter per chat, or Day 25's time-ordered ids, will do.

Offline users: if no server holds the receiver, the message waits in their inbox and a push notification goes out (Day 62). On reconnect the phone sends, per chat, the last sequence number it has and gets everything after it, so a gap fills itself.

Ticks: one tick once the server has saved the message, two once the receiver's phone acks it, blue once they open the chat. Acks travel back as small messages; in a group, two ticks means every member's phone has acked.

Groups: the message is saved once and fanned out to each member's channel, Day 67's fan-out on write, fine for a hundred members. Photos go straight from the phone to blob storage with a presigned URL, the message carries only the link, and receivers fetch it through a CDN (Day 74).

Presence ("online", "last seen") comes from the connection itself and its heartbeats, held in memory, not a database write on every heartbeat. Wrap up with the bottlenecks: connections per server, hot groups, and reconnect storms after a deploy (backoff with jitter, Day 39).
blocks.say: Each phone holds a WebSocket to a connection server that subscribes to its user's channel; the chat service gives each message a per-chat sequence number, saves it in a store sharded by chat id, then publishes it to each member's channel, keeps it in an inbox with a push notification for anyone offline, and phones catch up by asking for everything after their last sequence number.
example: Asha's phone holds a WebSocket to connection server 1, Ravi's to server 3, which subscribed to the channel user:ravi when he connected.
Asha sends "Reached Pune" in chat 42. The chat service gives it sequence 118 in chat 42, saves it in chat 42's shard and acks Asha's phone: one tick.
It publishes the message to user:ravi; server 3 pushes it down Ravi's socket, his phone acks, and the ack flows back to Asha: two ticks. Ravi opens the chat, a read receipt follows: blue ticks.
Had Ravi's phone been off, nobody would hold user:ravi: the message waits in his inbox and a push goes out. When he reconnects, his phone says "chat 42: I have up to 117" and receives 118 onward.
In a group of five, the same message is saved once and published to four members' channels; Asha sees two ticks only when all four phones have acked.

tasks.text: Read the primary from Understanding the Problem through High-Level Design, then Potential Deep Dives 1 to 3 (about 30 minutes). Write one line each for: chat server, inbox, client ack, heartbeat, and why the design routes messages through pub/sub.

Day 32's first 15 minutes, on paper: requirements and estimates. Assume 500 million daily users who each send 40 messages a day of about 100 bytes, a 3× peak, 200 million phones online at once, and 100,000 connections per server. Check: about 230,000 messages a second on average (about 700,000 at peak), 2 TB of message text a day before copies, and 2,000 connection servers.

About 45 minutes, in d76.py: `PubSub` (a dict from channel to a list of callbacks, with subscribe, unsubscribe, and publish returning how many received it); `ConnectionServer(pubsub)` with `connect(user, phone)`, where a phone is a list of received (chat, seq, text), subscribing to "user:<name>", and `disconnect(user)`; and `ChatService` with members per chat, a counter per chat, every message saved per chat, and an inbox per user. `send(chat, sender, text)` saves the message with the next sequence number, publishes it to every other member, and puts it in a member's inbox when the publish reached nobody; `sync(user, chat, last_seq)` returns the messages after last_seq. Test: Asha on one server and Ravi on another receive 1, 2, 3 in order; Meera, offline, gets nothing, then after connecting and syncing from 0 gets all three; a chat of four delivers each message to three phones.

Out loud, about 10 minutes: walk the example's message through one tick, two ticks and blue ticks, then say what changes in a group of five. Then explain "last seen" without writing to the database on every heartbeat.

About 10 minutes, one user on several devices: change d76.py so `connect(user, device, phone)` subscribes to "user:<name>:<device>" and the service knows each user's devices. `send` publishes to every device of every member, including the sender's other devices but not the one that sent it, and each device syncs on its own from its own last sequence number. Test: Asha sends from her laptop; her phone gets it, the laptop doesn't get it back, and Ravi's phone and laptop each get it once.

selftest.q: A phone was off for a day. How does it catch up without missing or repeating messages?

blocks.title: Backtracking: making a square from matchsticks
blocks.builds_on: Days 69 to 76 · Backtracking
points: Earlier problems chose whether each item is in or out. Some ask which of several groups each item goes into: with k groups each item has k choices, so k^n leaves before pruning.
Pruning decides whether that finishes in time: check that a choice still fits before recursing, and order the items so dead ends show up near the root.
Before any search, look for cheap checks on totals and sizes that make the answer impossible, and return at once.

matchsticks-to-square: What must every side's length be, and which single stick could rule out a square straight away?
Try placing the longest sticks first: why does that reach dead ends sooner?

blocks.say: Each side must be total ÷ 4, so I return False if the total isn't divisible by 4 or a stick is longer than a side, then backtrack stick by stick, longest first, putting each on any side with room: O(4^n) at worst, far less with the checks.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): colour a map of five city wards, A to E, with red, green and blue so that neighbouring wards differ. A borders B and C; B borders C and E; C borders E; D borders only E.

Each ward in turn tries red, then green, then blue, and a colour is checked against the coloured neighbours before recursing. A gets red. B: red clashes with A, so green. C: red and green clash with A and B, so blue. D: no coloured neighbour yet, so red.
E: red clashes with D, green with B, blue with C. Dead end: E has no colour left, so undo D's red and try its next colour.
D gets green, and now E can take red (its neighbours are green, blue and green). Done: A red, B green, C blue, D green, E red, after 7 calls.
Three colours give each ward 3 choices, at most 3^5 = 243 leaves; the check before each call cut almost all of them, and the search stopped at the first full answer.

blocks.title: Tries (hard): Word Search II
blocks.builds_on: Days 67 and 68 · Tries, and Day 74 · Backtracking on a grid
first: Timer: 40 minutes. Stuck when it rings: one line in My notes on where, then take the help on its row one step at a time. Show the answer last and watch only the idea in its Video, then close it and code it from blank. Show the answer turns its bookmark on for you.
points: You built a trie (Day 67) and searched a grid letter by letter, marking each cell on the way in and unmarking it on the way out (Day 74). This hard combines them: find every word from a list that the grid can spell.

search-for-word-ii: Step 1, brute force: run your Day 74 search once per word. With w words, an m × n grid and words of length L, roughly how many steps is that, and what is repeated between words that share a start, such as "oath" and "oat"?
Step 2: what if one walk from each cell checked every word at once? As you step onto a letter, what tells you straight away that no word continues this way?
Step 3: when the walk reaches a node that ends a word, how do you record it only once, even if the grid spells it twice?
Step 4, speed: once a word is found, can its trie nodes be cut so later walks stop sooner? Trace a 2 × 2 grid of a, b over c, d with the words ab, abd, ca and dc on paper first.

blocks.say: I put every word in a trie and run one DFS from each cell, stepping only to a neighbour whose letter is a child of the current trie node, marking the cell on the way in and unmarking it on the way out; when a node ends a word I record it and clear its word so it's found once, and I prune trie nodes that are used up.
example: Practice problem (not NeetCode 250, LeetCode 648): a dictionary has the roots cat, bat, rat and ca. Replace each word of "the cattle was rattled by the battery" with its shortest root, and leave a word with no root as it is.

Put the four roots in one trie (Day 67). For each word, walk the trie from its first letter: stop at the first node that ends a root, since that is the shortest, or the moment the trie has no child for the next letter.

"the": the trie has no child t at its root, so stop after one check and keep the word. "cattle": c, a, and "ca" ends there: replace it with ca, never reading t, t, l, e. "was" stops at once, and "by" after b, as no root continues with y.
"rattled": r, a, t ends "rat". "battery": b, a, t ends "bat". Result: "the ca was rat by the bat".
One walk checks every root at once, and a word costs at most the length of its root, not one comparison per root: with thousands of roots, that is the saving.

blocks.title: Machine coding: Splitwise, with split rules and balances
blocks.builds_on: Day 16 · Strategy, Day 21 · the machine-coding playbook, Day 42 · money as whole numbers, Day 2 · dataclasses, and Day 63 · a machine coded test first
points: Splitwise tracks shared spending: who paid, how each bill is split, and who owes whom. Requirements first: users, groups, expenses split equally, by exact amounts or by percentages, each user's balances, and a way to settle up.

Entities: User, Group and Expense (who paid, the amount, the people in it and how it is split), as dataclasses (Day 2), plus an ExpenseService that holds the balances. A thin main() drives it (Day 21).

Money in paise, as whole numbers (Day 42 kept whole rupees): floats can't hold 0.1 exactly. ₹1,000 split three ways is 100,000 paise: 33,333 each, and the 1 paisa left over goes to the first person, so the parts add up exactly.

Each split type is a Strategy (Day 16) behind one method, `split(total, users, values)`, returning {user: paise}. EqualSplit ignores values; ExactSplit checks the amounts add up to the total; PercentSplit checks the percentages add up to 100. A new type is a new class, never a new elif.

Balances: `owes[(a, b)]` is what a owes b. For each person in an expense other than the payer, add their share to what they owe the payer, netted against anything the payer already owes them, so a pair never holds debts both ways.
Validation raises ValueError with a clear message: a negative amount, a payer outside the group, exact amounts that don't add up.
Write the tests first, as on Day 63: they pin down the rounding and the netting before any class exists.

Step up to name: simplify debts. Work out each person's net (what they are owed minus what they owe), then repeatedly let the biggest debtor pay the biggest creditor; n people settle in at most n − 1 payments.
blocks.say: I model users, groups and expenses as dataclasses, keep money in paise, make each split type a Strategy that validates and returns paise per user, and keep pairwise balances netted both ways in a service; simplifying debts nets each person and pairs the biggest debtor with the biggest creditor.
example: A Goa trip: Asha, Ravi and Meera. Asha pays ₹1,200 for the hotel, split equally: Ravi and Meera each owe Asha ₹400.
Ravi pays ₹300 for a cab, split exactly: Asha ₹100, Meera ₹200. Asha's ₹100 nets against Ravi's ₹400 debt to her: Ravi now owes Asha ₹300. Meera owes Ravi ₹200.
Meera pays ₹1,000 for dinner, by percentages 50, 30 and 20: Asha ₹500, Ravi ₹300, Meera ₹200 (her own share, owed to nobody).

Netting: Asha owed Meera 500 against Meera's 400 to her, so Asha owes Meera ₹100; Ravi owed Meera 300 against her 200 to him, so Ravi owes Meera ₹100. Balances: Ravi → Asha 300, Asha → Meera 100, Ravi → Meera 100.
Nets: Asha +200, Ravi −400, Meera +200, adding up to 0. Simplified, Ravi pays Asha ₹200 and Meera ₹200: two payments instead of three.

tasks.text: 10 minutes, before any code: write the requirements as a list, then the entities, the `split(total, users, values)` interface, and the service's method names (`add_expense`, `balances_of`).

About 15 minutes, tests first in test_d77.py: an equal split of 100,000 paise three ways gives 33,334, 33,333 and 33,333; exact amounts that don't add up raise ValueError; 50/30/20 of 125,000 paise gives 62,500, 37,500 and 25,000; the example's three expenses leave Ravi owing Asha ₹300, Asha owing Meera ₹100 and Ravi owing Meera ₹100. Run them with `uv run --with pytest pytest test_d77.py`: they fail.

About 45 minutes in d77.py, in slices that each run (Day 21): the dataclasses, the three split Strategies, then ExpenseService with add_expense and the netted balances, until every test passes. A `main()` replays the Goa trip and prints each balance.

blocks.title: Context windows: their limits, and tricks for long inputs
blocks.builds_on: Day 73 · prefill, decode and the KV cache's memory per token, Day 63 · positional encodings and RoPE, Day 64 · nanoGPT's learnt position table, Day 57 · the causal mask, and Day 52 · attention's n × n table of scores
points: The context window is the most tokens a model takes in at once, prompt and answer together: 1,024 for GPT-2, 4,096 for Llama 2, 128,000 or more for many models today. Past it, older text must be cut, summarised or left out.

Compute: attention scores every pair of tokens (Day 52), an n × n table per head per layer. At 4,096 tokens that is about 16.8 million scores; at 131,072 it is about 17.2 billion: 32 times the text costs 1,024 times the work.

Memory: the KV cache (Day 73) grows by one K row and one V row per token in every layer, 2 × layers × d × bytes. A 7B model with 32 layers and d = 4,096 in fp16 needs 0.5 MiB a token: 2 GiB at 4,096 tokens, 64 GiB at 131,072, far more than its 13 GiB of weights.

Positions: a learnt table like GPT-2's (Day 64) has no row past its last position. RoPE (Day 63) can compute any position, but the model never saw such large distances in training and quality falls apart. Position interpolation squeezes the new positions into the trained range and fine-tunes briefly: LLaMA went from 2,048 to 32,768 tokens in about 1,000 steps.

Sliding-window attention: each token attends only to the w tokens nearest it, so a layer costs O(n · w) instead of O(n²), and the cache can stop growing at w rows. Layers stack: after k layers information can travel k × w tokens, so Mistral 7B's w = 4,096 over 32 layers reaches about 131,000.
A decoder's window looks only back, with Day 57's causal mask. Today's Deep-ML window looks both ways, a radius on each side, as an encoder can.

Long isn't the same as used: in "Lost in the Middle" (2023), models answered best when the needed fact sat at the start or the end of a long prompt and worst when it sat in the middle. Put instructions and key facts at the ends.
When the material is far bigger than any window, put only the relevant pieces in the prompt instead: retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which month 4 builds.
blocks.say: A context window is limited by attention's O(n²) scores and the KV cache's O(n) memory, about 0.5 MiB a token for a 7B model, and by positions the model never trained on; sliding-window attention cuts each layer to O(n · w) while stacked layers still reach k × w back, position interpolation stretches RoPE, and past that I retrieve instead of stuffing the prompt.
example: A 7B model like Llama 2: 32 layers, d = 4,096, fp16 at 2 bytes a number.
KV cache per token: 2 (K and V) × 32 × 4,096 × 2 bytes = 524,288 bytes = 0.5 MiB.
A 4,096-token chat needs 2 GiB of cache. Stretched to 131,072 tokens: 64 GiB, about five times the model's 13 GiB of weights, for one user.

Scores at 131,072 tokens: about 17.2 billion per head per layer. A window of 4,096 cuts that to about 537 million, 32 times fewer, since each token scores w keys instead of n, and the cache can stop at 4,096 rows: 2 GiB again.
Mistral's 32 layers with w = 4,096 can still carry information from about 131,000 tokens back, but only by passing it from layer to layer.

In d77.py, about 5 minutes: compute the KV cache per token and at 4,096 and 131,072 tokens for 32 layers, d = 4,096 and 2 bytes (0.5 MiB, 2 GiB and 64 GiB), and the pairs scored at 131,072 tokens with and without a 4,096 window (about 17.2 billion and 537 million).

Here window_size is a radius on both sides with no causal mask: token i attends to keys max(0, i − w) to min(n − 1, i + w), both ends included. Loop over i: score Q[i] against that slice of K, divide by scale_factor, or by √d_k with d_k = Q.shape[1] when it is None, softmax over that slice only (subtract its largest score before `np.exp`, as on Day 57), and mix the same slice of V. Return the (n, d_v) array. It runs in the browser and numpy is fine. Pass its tests, then read its Learn tab.

blocks.title: Backtracking: splitting numbers into k equal groups
blocks.builds_on: Days 69 to 77 · Backtracking, and Day 7 · a first feel for dynamic programming
first: One problem today, so start with the Revise row: re-solve what is due from a blank file and rate each, for about 25 minutes. Then give the rest of the block to today's problem; anything left in the Revise row shows again tomorrow.
points: Pruning cuts a branch before you walk it. Three cheap kinds: a bound (what is left can no longer reach the target, or has passed it), a check on totals before any search, and symmetry (two choices that lead to the same sub-search: try only one of them).
Order the items largest first. Big items fail soonest, so dead ends show up near the root, where one cut removes the most leaves.
Pruning doesn't change the worst case (k groups still give up to k^n leaves), but on real inputs it is the difference between instant and hopeless. Count your calls on a small input to see it.

partition-to-k-equal-sum-subsets: What must every group's sum be, and what makes the answer False before any search?
If two groups are both still empty, does it matter which one gets the next number? How does that cut the tree?
Optional step up: fill one group at a time, keep the used numbers in a bitmask, and cache on the mask with functools.cache (Day 7).

blocks.say: Each group must sum to total ÷ k, so I return False if that isn't whole or a number is bigger; then I sort largest first and backtrack number by number into any group with room, skipping a group whose sum equals one already tried, which also stops an empty group being tried twice; worst case O(k^n), and a bitmask with a cache gives O(n · 2^n).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): pick parcels of 2, 3, 5, 6 and 8 kg that weigh exactly 21 kg in all. Each parcel is in or out; count the calls each way.
Plain order, 2 first: the search takes 2, 3, 5 and 6 (16), finds no room for the 8, backs up through the small parcels and finds 2 + 5 + 6 + 8 after 20 calls.
Largest first, with a bound: before going on, check that what is left can still reach the target, and skip a parcel heavier than what is left.
8 (13 left), 6 (7 left), 5 (2 left); 3 is too heavy, so skip it; 2 brings it to 0. Found: 8 + 6 + 5 + 2 = 21 after 6 calls.
The bigger the input, the bigger the gap: parcels 1 to 10 kg with a target of 54 take 1,033 calls in plain order and 10 sorted largest first.

blocks.title: Post-training 1: supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
blocks.builds_on: Day 70 · pre-training on next-token cross-entropy, Day 66 · tokenisation, and Day 49 · a language model trained with F.cross_entropy
points: A pre-trained model (Day 70) continues text; it doesn't follow instructions. Post-training turns it into an assistant, in two steps: supervised fine-tuning (today), then preference tuning (Day 80).

SFT trains on example conversations: an instruction and the response we want, written or checked by people. The loss is the same next-token cross-entropy as pre-training, only on far less, far cleaner data.

A chat template turns a conversation into one token sequence, with special tokens for each role and for the end of a turn, e.g. <|user|> … <|end|> <|assistant|> … <|end|>. At inference the same template must be used, or the model sees a format it never learnt.

Loss only on the response: the prompt's tokens get the label -100, which PyTorch's cross_entropy skips (ignore_index), so the model learns to answer, not to predict the user's words. The assistant's end-of-turn token keeps its label, so the model learns when to stop.

Quality over quantity: LIMA (2023) fine-tuned a 65B model on about 1,000 carefully chosen examples and its answers held up well against models tuned on far more data. SFT mostly teaches format and style; the knowledge came from pre-training.
Forgetting: training on a narrow set can erase skills the base model had. Mix in general data, use a small learning rate and few epochs, and check the old skills after training.
Cost: SFT updates every weight, so a 7B model needs memory for its weights, gradients and Adam's two moments (Day 42), many times the 13 GiB of weights. Day 85's LoRA trains a small add-on instead.
blocks.say: SFT trains a pre-trained model on instruction and response pairs, rendered with a chat template of role tokens, using the same next-token loss but masked to the response tokens with -100 so it learns to answer and when to stop; a thousand excellent examples beat a million noisy ones, and I watch for forgetting.
example: A two-turn chat: the user asks "what is the capital of india", the assistant says "new delhi", the user asks "and of goa", the assistant says "panaji".
Template, one token per word: <|user|> what is the capital of india <|end|> <|assistant|> new delhi <|end|> <|user|> and of goa <|end|> <|assistant|> panaji <|end|>. 20 tokens.
Labels: -100 for every user token and both <|assistant|> markers; the real token for new, delhi, <|end|>, panaji, <|end|>. 5 of the 20 tokens are in the loss.

With random logits over the 14 distinct tokens (seed 0), cross_entropy with ignore_index=-100 gives 3.3047, the plain mean of −log p over those 5 tokens. Without the mask it is 2.98: the prompt's tokens dilute it.
Training then lowers only those 5 terms; nothing pushes the model to predict what the user will say.

blocks.title: Heap / Priority Queue: the kth largest in a stream, and smashing stones
blocks.builds_on: Day 7 · heaps, and Day 55 · heapq in a hard
points: A heap keeps the smallest item on top, ready in O(1), and adds or removes one item in O(log n). It is a complete binary tree stored in a list, where every parent is no bigger than its children (Day 7).

Python's heapq works on a plain list: `heappush(h, x)`, `heappop(h)` returns the smallest, `h[0]` peeks without removing, `heapify(h)` turns a list into a heap in O(n), and `heapreplace(h, x)` pops then pushes in one O(log n) step.

heapq is a min-heap only. For the largest on top, push −x and negate it on the way out. To order by a key, push a tuple (key, tie-break, item): tuples compare item by item, and a unique tie-break such as an arrival number keeps two equal keys from ever comparing the items.
Use a heap when you need the smallest or largest again and again while items keep arriving or leaving. Once only: min() in O(n). Everything in order: sort.

kth-largest-integer-in-a-stream: How many numbers do you really need to keep to answer every add, and which of them must sit on top?
last-stone-weight: Each turn needs the two heaviest stones and may put one back: which heapq calls make a turn O(log n), and what do you return when no stone is left?

blocks.say: For the kth largest in a stream I keep a min-heap of only the k largest seen, popping when it grows past k, so the top is the answer: O(log k) per add. For Last Stone Weight I push negated weights, pop the two heaviest, push back their difference if it isn't 0, and return the last stone or 0: O(n log n).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): a hospital's emergency room sees the most severe patient first, and among equal severity, whoever arrived first.
Push (−severity, arrival number, name): Asha severity 2 arrives 0th, Ravi 5 arrives 1st, Meera 5 arrives 2nd, Kabir 3 arrives 3rd. Negating makes heapq's smallest the most severe.
h[0] is (−5, 1, "Ravi"): he is next. Two pops give Ravi, then Meera: same severity, and the arrival number breaks the tie without ever comparing names.
Dev arrives 4th with severity 4: push (−4, 4, "Dev"), O(log n). The next pops are Dev, Kabir, Asha.
Each push and pop is O(log n), peeking is O(1); sorting the waiting list again at every arrival would cost O(n log n) each time.

blocks.title: Whiteboard LLD: an ATM in 20 minutes
blocks.builds_on: Day 37 · State, Day 72 · Chain of responsibility, Day 42 · a vending machine whose greedy change can fail, Day 46 · sagas and compensating steps, and Day 21 · the machine-coding playbook
points: Some rounds want a design on a whiteboard in about 20 minutes, not running code: requirements, the classes and how they talk, one flow walked through, then what changes. An ATM is a classic one.

Requirements: insert a card, enter the PIN (three wrong tries keep the card), choose withdraw, deposit or balance, take the cash and the card. Out of scope, say so: the bank's own systems sit behind a `BankService` interface.
Classes: ATM (the machine, holding its state), Card, Account, BankService (checks the PIN, holds and debits money), CashDispenser, and the notes it holds.

The ATM's State (Day 37): Idle → CardInserted → Authenticated → back to Idle. Each state is a class with insert_card, enter_pin, withdraw and eject_card; a call that makes no sense in a state (withdrawing before the PIN) is refused by that state, with no if-chains on a status field.

The dispenser is a Chain of responsibility (Day 72): a ₹500 handler gives as many notes as it can and passes the rest to ₹200, then ₹100. A new note is a new handler in the chain. Greedy can fail with a limited stock, as Day 42's change did, so plan the whole amount before any note moves.

Order of a withdrawal: plan the notes, ask the bank to debit, then dispense. If dispensing fails after the debit, the bank reverses it with a compensating credit (Day 46's saga); no transaction spans the ATM and the bank (Day 75).
blocks.say: I model the ATM with the State pattern, Idle, CardInserted, Authenticated, so each state refuses calls that make no sense, put the bank behind an interface, and dispense notes through a Chain of responsibility from ₹500 down to ₹100, planning the whole amount before the bank debits and anything leaves the machine.
example: Asha withdraws ₹3,800. The ATM is Authenticated; the request goes to the dispenser chain, with plenty of every note.
₹500 handler: 3,800 ÷ 500 = 7 notes, 300 left, passed on. ₹200: 1 note, 100 left. ₹100: 1 note, 0 left.
Plan {₹500: 7, ₹200: 1, ₹100: 1}: nothing left over, so the bank debits ₹3,800, the notes come out and the state goes back to Idle when the card is taken.
Now a nearly empty machine: one ₹500, three ₹200, no ₹100, and ₹600 asked. Greedy takes the ₹500 and is left with ₹100 it can't pay, though three ₹200 notes would do.
Because the plan comes first, the ATM refuses (or tries a fuller search) before the bank debits anything; no money is taken and no notes are stuck.

selftest.q: Kth Largest Element in a Stream: what does the heap hold, and why is its top the answer?
selftest.a: A min-heap of only the k largest numbers seen. Its smallest, on top, is the kth largest overall. Each add pushes, then pops if the heap holds more than k: O(log k).

selftest.q: heapq only gives the smallest. How do you get the largest out first?
selftest.a: Push −x and negate the value when you pop it.

selftest.q: Why push (key, arrival number, item) rather than (key, item)?
selftest.a: When two keys are equal, tuples compare the next field. A unique arrival number settles the tie, keeps first-come order, and stops Python comparing items that can't be compared.

selftest.q: An ATM holds ₹500, ₹200 and ₹100 notes. Which patterns fit the machine and the dispenser, and what must happen before the bank debits?
selftest.a: State for the machine (Idle, CardInserted, Authenticated) and a Chain of responsibility for the notes. The dispenser must plan the whole amount first, because greedy can fail with a limited stock.

selftest.q: Day 63: how does RoPE put a token's position into attention?
selftest.a: It rotates each pair of numbers in q and k by an angle proportional to the position, so the score of q and k depends only on how far apart the two tokens are.

blocks.title: Heap / Priority Queue: the k closest points, and the kth largest in an array
blocks.builds_on: Day 79 · heapq
points: Top k of n: keep a heap of only k items, the best k so far, with the worst of them on top so it is the one thrown out. Each item costs O(log k): O(n log k) time and O(k) memory.
Sorting everything is O(n log n) and the right first answer to say. The heap wins when k is much smaller than n, or when the items arrive one at a time and can't all be held.

k-closest-points-to-origin: Do you need the square root to compare two distances?
heapq keeps the smallest on top. To keep the k closest and throw out the farthest, what do you push?
kth-largest-element-in-an-array: Optional step up: quicksort's partition puts one value in its final place in O(n). How could you use it to find the kth largest in O(n) on average, without sorting the rest?

blocks.say: For the k closest points I push (−squared distance, point) and pop whenever the heap grows past k, so the farthest kept point is always on top: O(n log k). For the kth largest I keep a min-heap of k, or use quickselect: partition around a pivot and recurse into the side that holds index n − k, O(n) on average and O(n²) at worst.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): sort [3, 1, 2, 6, 4, 5], where every number is at most k = 2 places from its sorted spot (like orders arriving slightly out of time order).
The smallest remaining number must be among the next k + 1 numbers, so keep a min-heap of k + 1 = 3. Push 3, 1, 2; the heap has 3, so pop the smallest: 1.
Push 6, pop 2. Push 4, pop 3. Push 5, pop 4. The input is done: drain the heap, 5 then 6.
Output 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Each number is pushed and popped once in a heap of at most 3: O(n log k), better than O(n log n) when k is small.

blocks.title: Post-training 2: preference tuning with RLHF and DPO
blocks.builds_on: Day 78 · supervised fine-tuning, Day 8 · the sigmoid and log loss, and Day 42 · training loops
points: After SFT (Day 78) the model answers, but not always the way people prefer. Writing the perfect answer is hard; choosing the better of two is easy. Preference data is exactly that: a prompt, a chosen answer and a rejected one.

RLHF, step 1: train a reward model, an LLM with a single score as output, so the chosen answer scores higher. Its loss is −log σ(r_chosen − r_rejected): scores 2.0 and 0.5 give 0.201; the wrong way round gives 1.701.

RLHF, step 2: the SFT model generates answers, the reward model scores them, and reinforcement learning (PPO) pushes the model towards higher scores. A KL penalty keeps it close to the SFT model, so it can't drift into gibberish that happens to score well.

Reward hacking: the model maximises the reward as measured, not what we meant, such as longer answers or flattery if the reward model happened to like them. Today's guide lesson covers this, so the block's own reading is shorter.

DPO (2023) skips the reward model and the RL loop. Its loss compares how much more likely the model makes each answer than a frozen reference (the SFT model): −log σ(β · ((log π_c − log ref_c) − (log π_r − log ref_r))).

β sets how strongly the model is held to the reference: with a bigger β the same move gives a bigger z and a lower loss, so the loss is satisfied by a smaller move and the model stays closer to the reference; a small β (0.1) lets it drift further. At the start the model equals the reference, so the loss is log 2 = 0.693; it falls as the chosen answer gains likelihood against the rejected one.

In practice: RLHF with PPO is powerful but costly (four models in memory: policy, reference, reward and value); DPO is one supervised-style loss on preference pairs, which is why many open models use it.
blocks.say: Preference tuning uses pairs of a chosen and a rejected answer: RLHF trains a reward model with −log σ(r_c − r_r) and then runs PPO with a KL penalty to the SFT model, which risks reward hacking; DPO skips both and directly raises the chosen answer's log-likelihood ratio over a frozen reference against the rejected one's, scaled by β, where a bigger β holds it closer to the reference.
example: One pair: "Suggest a weekend trip from Pune". Chosen: a short list with travel times. Rejected: a long, vague paragraph. Use β = 0.1, and log-probabilities of the whole answer.
At the start the model is the reference: chosen −12 vs −12, rejected −15 vs −15. Both differences are 0, so z = 0 and the loss is −log σ(0) = 0.693.
After some steps: chosen −10 (reference −12), rejected −17 (reference −15). z = 0.1 × ((−10 + 12) − (−17 + 15)) = 0.1 × 4 = 0.4, loss 0.513.

Had training gone the wrong way, chosen −14 and rejected −13: z = −0.4, loss 0.913. With β = 0.5, half that move (chosen −11, rejected −16, a move of 2 instead of 4) already gives z = 1.0 and a loss of 0.313, lower than 0.513: a bigger β is satisfied by a smaller move, so the model stays closer to the reference.

selftest.q: K Closest Points to Origin: what do you push, and why no square root?
selftest.a: (−(x² + y²), point), popping when the heap holds more than k, so the farthest kept point is on top. The square root doesn't change the order, so comparing squared distances is enough.

selftest.q: Kth Largest Element in an Array: heap or quickselect, and their costs?
selftest.a: A min-heap of k: O(n log k) time, O(k) memory. Quickselect: O(n) on average and O(n²) at worst, unless the pivot is random.

selftest.q: A reward model scores the chosen answer 2.0 and the rejected 0.5. What is its loss, and what does training do?

selftest.q: What does β do in DPO?
selftest.a: It scales the log-likelihood ratios inside the sigmoid. A bigger β makes the loss fall with a smaller move, so the model stays closer to the reference; a small β lets it drift further for the same preference.

selftest.q: Day 66: why do models trip on how many r's are in "strawberry"?

task-scheduling: Which task should run next when several are ready?
A task that just ran must wait out its cooldown: keep it aside with the time it is ready again, and move it back into the heap when that time comes.
Optional step up: can you work out the answer from the most frequent task's count alone, without simulating?
design-twitter-feed: To compare tweets from different users by how recent they are, what should each tweet store, without using the clock?
getNewsFeed wants the 10 most recent tweets across a user and everyone they follow. If each person's tweets are kept in time order, which earlier shape is this?

blocks.say: For Task Scheduler I push negated counts, run the most frequent ready task each tick and park it in a queue with the time it is ready again: O(time). For Design Twitter each tweet takes a global counter, follows are a set per user, and the feed merges each followee's newest tweets with a heap of one candidate per person, stopping at 10.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): a payment service sends webhooks to a merchant whose server is down until second 4. A failed webhook is parked and retried after 1 second, then 2, then 4. In what order do the tries happen?
Park every webhook in a min-heap of (ready time, id), the retry queue of Day 62's notifier, so the next try is always on top. W1 arrives at second 0 and W2 at second 1: push (0, W1) and (1, W2).
t = 0: W1 fails, push (1, W1). t = 1: W1 comes first (the id breaks the tie), fails, push (3, W1); W2 fails, push (2, W2). t = 2: W2 fails, push (4, W2). t = 3: W1 fails, push (7, W1).
t = 4: W2 succeeds. Nothing is ready at 5 or 6, so jump the clock straight to the top's time, 7, where W1 succeeds.
Each park and each try is O(log n), and jumping to the top's ready time means waiting costs nothing, however long the delays grow.

blocks.title: Search basics: the inverted index, and tries for prefixes
blocks.builds_on: Day 67 · tries and fan-out, Day 41 · sharding and partition keys, Day 68 · when an index can't help, such as a LIKE that starts with a wildcard, and Day 53 · LSM trees merging sorted files
points: Searching "cheap goa hotels" with LIKE '%goa%' reads every row: an index can't help a LIKE that starts with a wildcard (Day 68). Search needs a different index.

An inverted index maps each word to its posting list: the ids of the documents that contain it, sorted. Building it: split the text into tokens, lower-case them (and often strip endings: hotels → hotel), then add each document's id to each token's list.
A query of two words intersects their lists. Both are sorted, so walk them together with two pointers: O(a + b), never comparing every pair.

Ranking by TF-IDF, by idea: a word that appears often in a document (term frequency) counts more, and a word found in nearly every document ("the", or "goa" on a Goa travel site) counts less: idf = log(N ÷ df).
Prefixes as you type: a trie (Day 67) of the known queries, each node keeping its top suggestions, answers "goa h…" in O(length of the prefix).
Updates: new documents go into small new index segments that are merged in the background, the LSM idea (Day 53), which is why a new document shows up in search a second or so later.

Sharding: by document, each shard indexes its own documents and a query goes to every shard, then the results are merged (the usual choice, as in Elasticsearch); by term, each word lives on one shard, so a query touches fewer shards but popular words make hot shards.
Search is a second copy of the data: the database stays the source of truth and the search cluster is fed from it, so it may lag a little.
blocks.say: Search uses an inverted index from each normalised token to a sorted posting list of document ids; a multi-word query intersects the lists with two pointers and ranks by TF-IDF, a trie of past queries serves suggestions, and I shard by document and query every shard, keeping the database as the source of truth.
example: Four documents: 1 "cheap flights to goa", 2 "cheap hotels in goa", 3 "flights to delhi", 4 "goa beach hotels".
Posting lists: cheap [1, 2], flights [1, 3], goa [1, 2, 4], hotels [2, 4], delhi [3].
"cheap goa": walk [1, 2] and [1, 2, 4] together: 1 matches, 2 matches, the first list ends. Result [1, 2]. "flights goa": [1].
IDF with N = 4, log10(N ÷ df): goa 0.12 (in 3 of 4), cheap and flights 0.30, delhi 0.60. A match on delhi counts about five times as much as one on goa.
Split over two shards by document (1 and 2, then 3 and 4): "cheap goa" goes to both, shard 1 returns [1, 2], shard 2 returns nothing, and the coordinator merges them.

points: Some heap problems run on a clock: items arrive at set times, and at each moment you choose among the ones that have already arrived. Two orders matter at once: the order things arrive in, and the order you serve them in.
Sort by arrival and walk a pointer along the sorted list. Each time the clock moves, push everything that has arrived into a heap keyed by the serving rule, then pop one.
When nothing is waiting, don't tick the clock forward one unit at a time: jump it straight to the next arrival.
Each item is pushed once and popped once: O(n log n) with the sort, and O(n) memory.

single-threaded-cpu: The answer is a list of the tasks' original positions, and sorting loses them. What do you carry along when you sort?
Two waiting tasks with the same processing time: the problem says which runs first. What goes in each heap entry so Python settles that tie the same way (Day 55)?

blocks.say: I sort the tasks by arrival with their original index, move a clock forward, push every task that has arrived into a min-heap of (processing time, index), pop one to run and add its time to the clock, and jump the clock to the next arrival when the heap is empty: O(n log n).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): you can attend one event a day, and an event (start, end) can be attended on any day from start to end. Events (1, 2), (1, 1), (2, 3) and (6, 6): how many can you attend?
Sort by start. Day 1: push the end days of the events that have started, (1, 2) and (1, 1): heap [1, 2]. Pop the earliest end, 1, and attend that event.
Day 2: (2, 3) starts, so push 3: heap [2, 3]. Pop 2 and attend. Day 3: pop 3 and attend. (An end day already past would be popped and thrown away.)
Day 4: the heap is empty, so jump the day straight to the next start, 6. Push 6, pop it, attend. Answer 4.
Attending (1, 2) on day 1 instead lets (1, 1) expire: only 3. The heap always serves the event that runs out soonest, and the jump skips the empty days 4 and 5.

blocks.title: Isolation levels: the anomalies each one prevents
blocks.builds_on: Day 75 · transactions and ACID, where isolation keeps transactions from seeing each other's half-done work, Day 26 · race conditions: count += 1 is a read, an add and a write, and Day 54 · SQL from Python with sqlite3
points: Day 75's I, isolation, at its strongest makes transactions running at once behave as if they ran one after another. That is slow, so databases offer weaker levels, each allowing some anomalies in return for speed.
Dirty read: you read a row another transaction changed but hasn't committed. It rolls back, and you acted on a value that never existed.

Non-repeatable read: you read a row twice in one transaction and get two values, because another transaction committed a change in between. Phantom: you run the same query twice and new rows appear, because another transaction inserted rows that match.
Lost update: two transactions read the same value, each changes it and writes it back, and the second write wipes out the first. It is Day 26's count += 1, now in a database.
The SQL standard's levels, weakest first: READ UNCOMMITTED allows all of them; READ COMMITTED stops dirty reads; REPEATABLE READ also stops non-repeatable reads; SERIALIZABLE stops everything.

Postgres: READ COMMITTED is the default, and each statement sees what was committed before that statement began. Its REPEATABLE READ reads one snapshot for the whole transaction, so it stops phantoms too, and its READ UNCOMMITTED acts as READ COMMITTED. MySQL's InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ.

At REPEATABLE READ the second writer waits for the first; if the first commits, Postgres aborts the second with a serialization failure (SQLSTATE 40001), and the app must retry the whole transaction. If the first rolls back, the second goes ahead. For a counter, UPDATE … SET n = n + 1 avoids the lost update at any level. Today's guide lesson covers the lost update and the retry loop, so the block's own reading is shorter.
blocks.say: Read committed stops dirty reads, repeatable read stops a row changing under me, and serializable makes concurrent transactions look one at a time; Postgres defaults to read committed, so for a read-modify-write I either do it in one UPDATE or run at a stronger level and retry on a serialization failure.
example: Asha's wallet holds ₹500. A refund (T1) and a cashback (T2) each add ₹100, at READ COMMITTED, by reading the balance, adding, and writing it back.
T1 reads 500. T2 reads 500. T1 writes 600 and commits. T2 writes 600 and commits. The wallet shows ₹600: ₹100 is lost, though every read saw committed data, so no dirty read happened.
At REPEATABLE READ, T2's write finds a row changed since its snapshot and fails with "could not serialize access due to concurrent update". The app retries T2, which now reads 600 and writes 700.
Or have both write it as one statement, UPDATE wallet SET balance = balance + 100: T2 waits for T1 to commit, then adds to the committed 600. ₹700 at the default level, with no retry.

selftest.q: In Single Threaded CPU, what goes in the heap, and what do you do when it is empty?
selftest.a: (processing time, original index) for every task that has arrived by the current time; the index settles ties the way the problem asks. When the heap is empty, jump the clock to the next task's arrival instead of ticking.

selftest.q: Name the four anomalies and the weakest Postgres level that stops each.
selftest.a: Dirty read: READ COMMITTED, Postgres's default and lowest. Non-repeatable read and phantom: REPEATABLE READ (the standard needs SERIALIZABLE for phantoms). Lost update: REPEATABLE READ, which aborts one writer so it retries, or an atomic UPDATE … SET n = n + 1 at any level.

selftest.q: Two transactions at REPEATABLE READ update the same row. What happens, and what must the app do?
selftest.a: The second waits for the first's row lock. If the first commits, the second fails with a serialization failure (SQLSTATE 40001, "could not serialize access due to concurrent update"), and the app must retry the whole transaction, which then reads the new value. If the first rolls back, the second goes ahead.

selftest.q: Day 62: in a notification system, why can't an OTP share one queue with a marketing campaign?
selftest.a: It would wait behind 10 million promotions. Each channel and priority gets its own queue (Day 39), so an OTP waits only behind other urgent messages, and a slow provider or a big campaign holds up only its own queue.

points: A greedy step with a heap: at each step take what the rule says is safest right now, and let the heap find it again in O(log k) after every change. With counts, whatever has the most left is usually the hardest to fit in later, so serve it early.
heapq is a min-heap, so push (-count, item) to get the largest count first (Day 79). After using an item, lower its count and push it back only if some is left.
Each of the n steps is a pop and a push on a heap of at most k distinct items: O(n log k) time and O(k) memory. For lowercase letters k ≤ 26, so that is O(n).

reorganize-string: Before building anything: in a string of n letters, how many copies of one letter can fit with a different letter between every two of them? Say when the answer is "".
You pop the letter with the most left and place it. If you push it straight back, the next pop may hand you the same letter. Where can it wait for one step?

blocks.say: I count the letters, return "" if one letter appears more than (n + 1) // 2 times, then repeatedly pop the letter with the most left from a max-heap, place it, and hold it out for one step before pushing it back, so it can't land twice in a row: O(n log k).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): three piles of 2, 4 and 6 stones. Each turn you take one stone from two different piles. How many turns can you play?
Keep the piles in a max-heap. Turn 1: pop the two biggest, 6 and 4, take one from each, push back 5 and 3: piles [2, 3, 5].
Turn 2: [2, 2, 4]. Turn 3: [1, 2, 3]. Turn 4: [1, 1, 2]. Turn 5: [1, 1], since the pile that reached 0 is not pushed back. Turn 6: empty. 6 turns.
Taking from the two smallest instead finishes the small piles first and leaves the big one alone: 4 turns.
Always taking from the biggest keeps the piles level, so no pile is stranded with stones and nothing to pair them with. 12 stones, 6 turns, the most possible.
