blocks.title: Backtracking (hard): N-Queens
blocks.builds_on: Days 69 to 78 · Backtracking, and Day 16 · checking a board's rows, columns and boxes
first: Timer: 40 minutes. Stuck when it rings: one line in My notes on where, then take the help on its row one step at a time. Show the answer last and watch only the idea in its Video, then close it and code it from blank. Show the answer turns its bookmark on for you.
points: You've built decision trees with choose, recurse and undo since Day 69, and checked a board's rows and columns with sets on Day 16. This hard combines them: place n queens on an n × n board so that none attacks another, and list every board.

n-queens: Step 1, brute force: try every way to put 8 queens on the 64 squares and check each board. How many boards is that? Now use one fact about any answer: how many queens can share a row?

Step 2: with one queen per row, recurse row by row and choose its column. Before placing, you need to know in O(1) whether that column or either diagonal is taken. What do you keep, and what do you add and remove around the recursive call?
Step 3: a square sits on two diagonals. Which numbers made from r and c name them, and how many of each are there on an n × n board?
Trace n = 4 on paper first: it has two boards. Build the rows of '.' and 'Q' only when you record a board, and record a copy.

blocks.say: I place one queen per row, recursing on the row and trying each column; three sets, columns, r − c and r + c, tell me in O(1) whether a square is attacked, I add to them before the call and remove after it, and at row n I record the board: about O(n!) time and O(n) extra space.
example: Practice problem (not NeetCode 250): bishops stand at (0, 1), (2, 3) and (3, 0) on a 4 × 4 board, as (row, column). Can a new bishop go at (1, 2) or at (2, 0) without being attacked?
A bishop moves along diagonals. Going down and right, row and column both grow by 1, so r − c stays the same; going down and left, r + c stays the same.
Store each bishop's two numbers: r − c gives −1, −1 and 3, so the set {−1, 3}; r + c gives 1, 5 and 3, so {1, 3, 5}.
(1, 2): r − c = −1 is in the first set, so (0, 1) and (2, 3) attack it, and r + c = 3 is in the second, so (3, 0) does too. (2, 0): r − c = 2 and r + c = 2, both free, so it is safe.
Each check is two set lookups, O(1), instead of walking the diagonals square by square. An n × n board has 2n − 1 values of each kind.

blocks.title: Design typeahead: the top suggestions for every prefix, fast
blocks.builds_on: Day 81 · search basics and a trie for prefixes, Day 67 · Tries, Day 74 · CDNs and caching at the edge, Day 41 · sharding and hot spots, Day 13 · caching, Day 11 · estimates, and Day 32 · the 45-minute design framework
points: The ask: as a user types into a search box, on Flipkart or Swiggy, show the top 5 completions of what's typed so far within about 100 ms of each keystroke. Rank by how often each query was searched; leave spelling fixes and personal ranking for later.

Requirements and numbers first (Day 32): 50 million daily users, 6 searches each, about 10 keystrokes a search: 50M × 6 × 10 / 86,400 ≈ 35,000 requests a second, about 105,000 at a 3× peak. Reads dwarf writes, and counts a day old are fine.

The structure: a trie of past queries (Day 81). A plain trie answers a prefix by walking to its node and then collecting everything below it, far too slow for "p". So store at each node the top k queries of its subtree, worked out ahead of time: a lookup is a walk of the prefix's length, then one ready list.

Building it: don't touch the trie on every search. Log each search; a daily batch job counts the logs, builds a fresh trie with the top k at each node, and swaps it in. Fresh enough beats exact; a smaller job every few minutes can add what is trending.
Serving: the trie sits in memory on the suggestion servers behind a load balancer (Day 6), or flattened into a key-value store of prefix → top k list that any server can read (Day 13).

Caching: the same prefixes repeat across millions of users, so let the browser keep recent answers and the CDN cache GET /suggest?q=pi for a few minutes, Day 74's edge caching. The client also waits for a short pause in typing before it asks, so fast typists send fewer requests.
Scaling: shard by prefix (Day 41), say a–m and n–z, but "s" and "p" get far more traffic than "x". Split hot ranges finer, by their first two letters, and add replicas for the hottest.
Latency budget (Day 11): of 100 ms, the network round trip takes most; the trie walk is microseconds. That is why caching close to the user matters more than a faster trie.
blocks.say: I keep past queries in a trie that stores the top k completions at every node, rebuilt by a daily batch job from the search logs; servers hold it in memory or as prefix-to-list in a key-value store, the browser and CDN cache popular prefixes, and I shard by prefix, splitting hot letters finer.
example: Yesterday's logs counted: pizza 50, paneer 40, pav bhaji 35, pizza hut 30, paratha 25, pista 20 and pizzeria 15. Keep the top 3 at each node.
Node "p" covers all seven: pizza, paneer, pav bhaji. Node "pi" covers the four pi- queries: pizza, pizza hut, pista.
Node "piz": pizza, pizza hut, pizzeria. Node "pa": paneer, pav bhaji, paratha.
The user types p, i, z: three requests, each a walk of 1 to 3 nodes and one list read. "p" and "pi" are so common that the CDN answers them without reaching a server.
Tonight's job counts today's searches and swaps in a new trie: if pista overtakes pizza hut today, "pi" shows pizza, pista, pizza hut tomorrow.

selftest.q: In Reorganize String, when is there no answer, and why?
selftest.a: When one letter appears more than (n + 1) // 2 times: even with every other letter placed between its copies, two of them would end up side by side.

selftest.q: N-Queens: what three sets do you keep, and what number names each diagonal?

selftest.q: Day 70: about how many training tokens does Chinchilla's rule suggest for a 7B model, and roughly how much compute is that?

selftest.q: Which pattern: a word dictionary whose search may contain '.', matching any one letter?

selftest.q: Which pattern: the kth largest of a stream of numbers, using O(k) memory?
selftest.a: A min-heap capped at k (Days 79 and 80): push each number and pop the smallest whenever the heap holds more than k; the root is then the kth largest. O(log k) per number.

selftest.q: Day 65: how does the Command pattern give undo and redo?

blocks.title: Heap / Priority Queue: a string with no three in a row, and a car's seats

first: Revise row first, about 15 minutes: re-solve from a blank file and rate each one. It may be fuller than usual, since what came due over the weekend waited for today; take the oldest first and leave the rest for tomorrow.
Then two problems, about 30 minutes each, each on a 25-minute timer. Stuck when it rings, take the help on its row one step at a time.
points: A heap keeps answering one question while things change: what is the biggest, or the soonest, right now. Today there are two kinds of change: counts that drop as you use them (Day 83), and a time line where things start and stop (Day 82).

longest-happy-string: The letter with the most left is the best choice, until it would make three in a row. What do you take instead for that one step, and what happens to the letter you popped first?
car-pooling: Only pickups and drop-offs change how many people are in the car. Take the trips in order of pickup: before each pickup, which earlier trips must you finish first?

What could hold the drop-off stops of the trips still in the car, so the soonest is always on top? Before each pickup, what do you pop, what running total do you keep beside it, and what does it cost if each trip is pushed and popped once?

Optional step up: the stops run from 0 to 1,000, small whole numbers, so an array can replace both the sort and the heap. Add the passengers at each pickup and subtract them at each drop-off in one array of stops, then add it up from left to right. What does the running total mean?

blocks.say: For Longest Happy String I pop the letter with the most left from a max-heap and, if it would make three in a row, use the next one instead and push both back; for Car Pooling I sort the trips by pickup, pop finished trips from a min-heap of drop-offs and check the riders never pass capacity, O(n log n), or add +p and −p into an array of stops and take a running sum, O(n + stops).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): you walk past buildings of heights 4, 2, 7, 6, 9, 14, 12. Going down is free; a climb of h costs h bricks or one ladder. With 5 bricks and 1 ladder, how far can you get?
Ladders should go on the biggest climbs. Walk forward and push each climb into a min-heap; whenever it holds more climbs than you have ladders, pop the smallest and pay for it in bricks.
2 → 7: climb 5, heap [5], the ladder covers it. 6 → 9: climb 3, heap [3, 5]: two climbs for one ladder, so pop 3 and pay 3 bricks, leaving 2.
9 → 14: climb 5, heap [5, 5]: pop a 5, but only 2 bricks are left. Stop at index 4, the building of height 9.
The heap only ever held the climbs given to ladders, the biggest so far, so each step costs O(log ladders).

blocks.title: Fine-tuning cheaply: LoRA adapters, and QLoRA
blocks.builds_on: Day 78 · supervised fine-tuning on instruction and response pairs, Day 36 · a layer is x @ W + b, Day 42 · Adam keeps two running averages per weight, and Day 73 · counting memory in bytes per number
points: Day 78's SFT updates every weight. For a 7B model in fp16 the weights take 14 GB, their gradients another 14 GB, and Adam's two running averages (Day 42) in fp32 another 56 GB: at least 84 GB before any activations, more than one 80 GB GPU.
LoRA (low-rank adaptation) freezes W and learns a small change beside it: h = W x + (α / r) · B A x. For a d × d matrix, A is r × d and B is d × r, with a small rank r such as 8.

The count: at d = 4,096, W holds 16,777,216 numbers, and A and B together 2 × 4,096 × 8 = 65,536, about 0.39%. Put LoRA on the query and value matrices of all 32 layers and you train about 4.2 million numbers, around 0.06% of a 7B model.

B starts at zero and A at small random numbers, so B A x = 0 at step 0: training starts from exactly the base model and moves away gently. The α / r factor keeps the update's size steady when you change r.

Why it works: the change fine-tuning needs tends to be low-rank, meaning a few directions capture most of it. B A is built from only r directions (its rank is at most r), and for most tasks that is enough.

Serving: merge the adapter, W' = W + (α / r) B A, and inference costs exactly what the base model costs. Or keep one base model in memory and swap small adapter files, a few MB each, per customer or per task.

QLoRA stores the frozen base in 4 bits (about 3.5 GB for 7B), turns each layer back into 16-bit numbers on the fly for its matrix multiply, and trains 16-bit LoRA adapters on top. A 7B fine-tune then fits on one consumer GPU. How 4-bit storage works is Day 87.
Trade-offs: LoRA can trail full fine-tuning on big shifts, such as a new language; raise r or add adapters to more matrices. QLoRA is slower per step because of the unpacking.
blocks.say: LoRA freezes the weights and learns a low-rank update B A beside each chosen matrix, with B starting at zero so training starts from the base model; at rank 8 that is well under 1% of the parameters, it merges back into W for free inference, and QLoRA keeps the frozen base in 4 bits so a 7B fine-tune fits on one GPU.
example: A 4 × 4 layer with a rank-1 adapter and α / r = 1: x = [1, 2, 0, 1], A = [1, 0, 1, 0] (1 × 4) and B = [1, 0, 2, 0]ᵀ (4 × 1).
At step 0, B is all zeros, so B (A x) = 0 and the layer outputs W x: exactly the base model.
After training: A x = 1·1 + 0·2 + 1·0 + 0·1 = 1, and B (A x) = [1, 0, 2, 0], which is added to W x. That took 4 multiplies for A x and 4 for B, against 16 for a full 4 × 4 change.
Merge: B A is the 4 × 4 matrix with rows [1, 0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 0, 0], [2, 0, 2, 0] and [0, 0, 0, 0], rank 1. (B A) x = [1, 0, 2, 0], the same as before, so W + B A serves with no extra step.
At this toy size the adapter holds 8 numbers against 16; at d = 4,096 and r = 8 it is 65,536 against 16.8 million.

selftest.a: Use the letter with the next most left for this one step, then push both back. If there is no second letter, stop: the string can't grow any longer.

selftest.a: The trips now in the car as (drop-off, passengers), a min-heap by drop-off. Before each pickup, taking trips in pickup order, pop every trip whose drop-off is at or before it and subtract its passengers; then add the new ones and check against capacity.

selftest.q: LoRA on a 4,096 × 4,096 matrix at rank 8: how many trainable numbers, and why does B start at zero?

selftest.q: What does QLoRA change compared with LoRA?
selftest.a: The frozen base model is stored in 4 bits instead of 16, about 3.5 GB for 7B instead of 14, and unpacked layer by layer for each matrix multiply; the LoRA adapters still train in 16 bits.

selftest.q: Day 72: in a chain of responsibility, what does each handler do with a request? Give one real use.

blocks.title: Graphs: a grid as a graph, and a made-up alphabet
blocks.builds_on: Day 6 · graphs, and Days 15 and 16 · grids
first: Revise row first, about 15 minutes: re-solve from a blank file and rate each one; anything you don't reach stays for tomorrow. Then Graphs begins with two Easy problems, about 25 minutes each, and the reading.
points: Day 6 in one breath: a graph is nodes and edges, stored as an adjacency list, a dict from each node to its neighbours. BFS visits nodes in rings of distance using a queue; DFS goes deep first using recursion or a stack. A visited set stops you going round in circles, so each node and edge is handled once: O(V + E).

A grid is a graph you don't have to build: each cell (r, c) is a node, and its neighbours are the four cells up, down, left and right. Loop over the four steps with `for dr, dc in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):`.
Check the bounds before you touch a neighbour: 0 <= r < rows and 0 <= c < cols. A step off the grid is not a neighbour, though some problems still care that you reached the edge.

On a grid, V is rows × cols and each cell has at most 4 edges, so a full BFS or DFS is O(rows × cols). The visited set can be a set of (r, c) pairs, or a mark written into the grid itself if you are allowed to change it.

island-perimeter: Each land cell has four sides. Which of them belong to the perimeter, and can you tell by looking only at that cell's four neighbours?
verifying-an-alien-dictionary: This one is tagged Graphs, but the alien order only ranks letters against each other. Do you need a search at all, or is one pass over neighbouring words enough?
Turn the alien order into a dict from letter to rank, so comparing two letters is O(1). Where do two neighbouring words first differ, and what decides it when one word is the start of the other?

blocks.say: I treat each cell as a node with four neighbours, check bounds before stepping and keep a visited set, so a grid search is O(rows × cols); for Island Perimeter I add 4 per land cell and subtract 1 for each side shared with land, and for the alien dictionary I rank the letters and compare each adjacent pair at their first different letter, where a longer word before its own prefix means unsorted.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): the fewest moves from S to E in the grid "S.#.", ".#..", "...E", stepping up, down, left or right, never onto #.
BFS from S at (0, 0), distance 0, marked visited. Pop it and push its open neighbours inside the grid, (1, 0) and (0, 1), at distance 1.
(1, 0) adds (2, 0) at 2; (0, 1) adds nothing, as (0, 2) and (1, 1) are walls. Then (2, 1) at 3, (2, 2) at 4, and (1, 2) and (2, 3) at 5.
(2, 3) is E: 5 moves. BFS pops cells in order of distance, so the first time it reaches E is the fewest moves.
Each of the 10 open cells entered the queue at most once, thanks to the visited set: O(rows × cols).

blocks.title: Concurrency for LLD 1: threads, locks and a thread-safe dict
blocks.builds_on: Day 26 · race conditions: count += 1 is a read, an add and a write, and a mutex around the critical section, Day 40 · deadlock and lock ordering, and Day 47 · the GIL, threads and ThreadPoolExecutor
points: LLD rounds now add a line such as "many users book at once". The classes stay the same; the question is which methods touch shared state, and how they stay correct when several threads call them together.

Day 26's race, now inside a class: `self.counts[key] = self.counts.get(key, 0) + 1` is a read, an add and a write. Two threads can both read 5 and both write 6, losing one update. The GIL (Day 47) doesn't save you: it keeps one bytecode step whole, not your three.
Check-then-act is the same bug in another shape: `if self.left > 0: self.left -= 1`. Two threads both see 1 seat left, both book, and the count reaches −1.
The fix: one `threading.Lock` per object, and every method that reads and then writes shared state does both inside `with self._lock:`. The with statement releases the lock even when the body raises.

Keep the locked part small: compute outside, lock only around the read-modify-write, and never make a slow call under the lock (a network call, a model call, a sleep), or every other thread waits behind it. Today's guide lesson covers that trap inside a database transaction, so the block's own reading is shorter.
One operation that needs two locks, such as moving a seat between two trains' quotas: take them in one fixed order, for example by id, so Day 40's deadlock can't form.
A single dict operation, d[k] = v or d.get(k), is safe in CPython, but a sequence of them is not. Say that in the interview, then lock anyway: it is clearer and doesn't depend on the interpreter.

Test it: hammer the object from 8 threads with ThreadPoolExecutor (Day 47) and check the totals. A race may not show on every run, so put `time.sleep(0)` between the read and the write to force a thread switch there.
blocks.say: Any method that reads shared state and then writes it is a critical section, so I give the object one threading.Lock and do the read-modify-write inside with self._lock, keep it short with no slow calls under it, take several locks in one fixed order, and prove it with a test that hammers the object from many threads.
example: An IRCTC Tatkal quota with 100 seats, and 400 booking attempts from 8 threads. `book()` checks `self.left > 0`, then takes a seat.
Without a lock: thread 1 sees left = 1 and is switched out; thread 2 sees 1, books, and left is 0; thread 1 resumes and books too. Left is −1: 101 tickets for 100 seats.
A run of the task below sold 106 tickets and left −6; the exact number changes from run to run, which is what makes races hard to catch.
With `with self._lock:` around the check and the take: exactly 100 sold, 0 left and 300 refusals, every run.
The cost: the check and the take now run one thread at a time. They take microseconds, so it doesn't matter; a payment call inside the lock would.

selftest.q: Island Perimeter: how do you get the perimeter without a search?
selftest.a: Each land cell adds 4, minus 1 for each of its sides that touches another land cell. A single pass over the grid, O(rows × cols).

selftest.q: Verifying an Alien Dictionary: what do you compare, and what is the edge case?
selftest.a: Each word with the next one: at their first different letter, the first word's letter must rank lower in the alien order. If there is no difference and the first word is longer, as in "apple" before "app", the list is not sorted.

selftest.q: On a 300 × 300 grid, how long does a full BFS take, and why might recursive DFS fail?
selftest.a: O(rows × cols): 90,000 cells, each with at most 4 edges. One big island can make recursive DFS 90,000 calls deep, far past Python's limit of about 1,000.

selftest.q: Why isn't self.counts[k] = self.counts.get(k, 0) + 1 safe with threads, even with the GIL?
selftest.a: It is a read, an add and a write. The GIL keeps one bytecode step whole, but a thread switch can land between the read and the write, so two threads both write 6 and one update is lost. A threading.Lock around the three steps fixes it.

selftest.q: Two threads lock quotas a and b in opposite orders. What can happen, and how do you prevent it?
selftest.a: Each holds one lock and waits forever for the other: a deadlock. Always take the locks in one fixed order, such as by id.

blocks.title: Graphs: who trusts whom, and islands on a grid
blocks.builds_on: Day 86 · Graphs: a grid as a graph, and Day 5 · recursion and the call stack
first: Revise row first, about 15 minutes: re-solve from a blank file and rate each one; anything you don't reach stays for tomorrow. Then three problems, each on its own timer: the Easy one 10 minutes, then the two Medium, 20 and 15. Stuck when one rings, take the help on its row one step at a time. If Number of Islands runs long, turn on Max Area of Island's bookmark instead, so it comes back in tomorrow's Revise row. The reading fits in the last 5 minutes.
points: A connected piece of a graph is a component: every node in it can reach every other. To count components, or measure each one, loop over every node and start a new search from each one not yet visited.

The search is Day 86's: BFS with a queue or DFS with recursion or a stack, four neighbours on a grid, bounds checked, and each cell marked when you first reach it, not when you pop it, so nothing enters twice. On a big grid, recursion can pass Python's limit of about 1,000 calls (Day 5), so a queue or your own stack is safer.

find-the-town-judge: In graph words, trusting someone is an edge out of you, and being trusted is an edge into you: each person's out-degree and in-degree. What must the judge's two counts be, and can one pass over the list count both for everyone?

Pop (1, 1): (0, 1) and (1, 0) are 1, so paint and push them; (2, 1) and (1, 2) are 0, so skip them. From those two, (0, 0), (0, 2) and (2, 0) get painted.
Result [[2, 2, 2], [2, 2, 0], [2, 0, 1]]: 6 cells changed. (2, 2) is 1, but it touches the region only corner to corner, so it stays.
If the new colour equals the start colour, return at once: painting would change nothing, so every cell would still look unvisited and the search would never end.

blocks.title: Quantisation: int8 and int4 weights, and what they cost
blocks.builds_on: Day 85 · QLoRA keeps the frozen base in 4 bits, Day 73 · the KV cache and memory in bytes per number, and Day 36 · a layer is x @ W + b
points: A weight in fp16 takes 2 bytes, so a 7B model is 14 GB; in int8 it is 7 GB, and in int4 3.5 GB. Smaller weights fit cheaper GPUs, and since decoding (Day 73) waits on weights streaming from memory, it runs faster too.
Absmax quantisation to int8: scale = 127 / max|w|, q = round(w × scale), clipped to −127…127. Store q as int8 plus the one scale. To use a weight, dequantise it: w ≈ q / scale.
The error is the rounding: at most half a step, 0.5 / scale. Symmetric int4 has only −7…7, so its steps are 18 times coarser and the error grows with them.

Outliers break a single shared scale: one weight of 24 among weights near 1 stretches the scale, so the small ones round to a few levels, or to 0. In LLMs the large outliers are in the activations, a few feature columns of the hidden states; the weights have milder ones, which the per-group scales below handle.

Fix it with more scales: one per row (per channel) or one per group of 64 or 128 weights. Each group pays for its own fp16 scale, so int4 with groups of 64 costs 4.25 bits a weight: 3.72 GB for 7B instead of 3.5.

Smarter methods pick the rounding with a little calibration data instead of rounding each weight alone: GPTQ fixes each rounding error by adjusting the weights not yet rounded, and AWQ protects the weights that meet the largest activations. Name them; the maths isn't needed.
The KV cache (Day 73) can be quantised too: for 4,096 tokens of a 7B model, int8 halves it from 2.15 GB to 1.07 GB.
The cost is accuracy: more at 4 bits than at 8, and more on small models. Measure on your own task, with perplexity or an eval set, before and after.
blocks.say: I quantise weights with a scale per group, q = round(w × 127 / max|w|) for int8, store the integers and the scale, and multiply back when using them; a 7B model goes from 14 GB to 7 or 3.5 GB, outliers are why one scale per tensor fails, and GPTQ or AWQ choose the rounding with calibration data to keep accuracy at 4 bits.
example: Make 2.4 an outlier of 24.0: the int8 scale drops to 5.29 and q = [3, −6, 0, 127, −4, 5]. Now 0.03 becomes 0 and 0.5 comes back as 0.567, even at 8 bits.
Groups of three: [0.5, −1.1, 0.03] gets its own scale, 127 / 1.1 = 115.45, and its largest error falls to 0.004. The outlier only spoils its own group.

points: Copying anything with shared parts or cycles needs a dict from each original to its copy (Day 43). Make the copy the first time you meet a node and store it before going further; meeting the node again, return the stored copy. The dict is also your visited set.

BFS finds the fewest steps from its start, because it takes nodes in order of distance (Day 86's maze). Keep (cell, distance) in the queue or loop level by level (Day 60): the first time you reach a cell is its shortest distance.
A graph given as nodes with neighbour lists is searched just like a grid; the neighbours come from the list instead of from four steps.
Both jobs are O(V + E): every node is copied or reached once, and every edge looked at once or twice.

clone-graph: What should happen when the search meets a node whose copy already exists? And when must a new copy go into the dict: before or after you copy its neighbours?
islands-and-treasure: Starting a BFS from every land cell costs O((rows × cols)²). Turn it round: where else could the search start?
What if every treasure chest goes into the queue at distance 0 before the search begins?

blocks.say: To clone a graph I DFS or BFS from the given node with a dict from each original to its copy, creating and storing the copy before visiting its neighbours so a cycle returns the stored copy, O(V + E); for Walls and Gates I put every treasure in the queue at distance 0 and run one BFS outwards, so each land cell gets its distance to the nearest treasure in O(rows × cols).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): copy a Python list that contains itself. a = [1, [2]], then a.append(a). A plain recursive copy never ends.
Keep memo, a dict from id(original) to its copy. copy(a) makes a new empty list c and stores memo[id(a)] = c before looking inside a, as Day 43 did with its old-to-new dict.
Copy 1: a number, kept as it is. Copy [2]: a new list, stored in memo, holding 2. The third item is a itself: id(a) is in memo, so append c instead of copying again.
c[2] is c: True, and c is a: False. The copy has the same shape, loop and all, and memo held 2 lists.
Python's copy.deepcopy works the same way: it keeps "a memo dictionary of objects already copied during the current copying pass". Storing the copy before recursing is what stops the loop.

blocks.title: Stream processing: Kafka partitions, consumer groups and windows
blocks.builds_on: Day 39 · message queues, retries and at-least-once delivery, Day 41 · partition keys and hot spots, and Day 18 · idempotency keys
points: Day 39's queue hands each message to one worker and deletes it once done. Kafka keeps a log instead: messages are appended to a topic and kept for days, and each reader tracks how far it has read, so many readers, and replays, come free.

A topic is split into partitions, each an ordered log on one broker (a Kafka server) and copied to others. The producer picks a partition from a key, hash(key) % partitions (Day 41), so all events of one rider or one order land in one partition, in order. Across partitions there is no order.

A consumer group shares the work: each partition goes to exactly one consumer in the group, so the partition count caps the parallelism. Twelve partitions and fifteen consumers leave three idle. Another group, such as analytics, reads the same events on its own.

Each consumer commits an offset, its place in each partition. Process first, then commit: a crash in between replays a few messages, which is at-least-once (Day 39). Make the handler idempotent (Day 18), such as an upsert keyed by the event id (insert the row, or update it if that id is already there), so a replay changes nothing.

Stream processing computes over events as they arrive: rides per city per minute, surge prices, fraud checks. A tumbling window is fixed and back to back (0–60 s, 60–120 s), so each event is in one; a hopping window has a fixed size but starts more often (60 s wide, every 30 s), so windows overlap.

Event time beats arrival time: phones go offline, so events arrive late and out of order. Window by when the event happened, keep each window open for a grace period, and decide what a later event does: update the result, or get dropped.
Hot keys hit partitions too: one huge seller's events all land in one partition. Add a suffix to that seller's key to spread it, giving up ordering across the pieces, or add partitions.
Reach for Kafka when one stream of events has many readers, needs replay or per-key order, or arrives at very high rates. A plain job queue is simpler when each task just needs one worker.
blocks.say: Kafka is a partitioned, replicated log: I key events so each entity's events stay ordered in one partition, scale reads with a consumer group of at most one consumer per partition, commit offsets after processing for at-least-once with idempotent writes, and aggregate over tumbling or hopping windows by event time with a grace period for late events.
example: A cab app sends ride events keyed by rider to a topic of 3 partitions. With zlib.crc32(rider) % 3: asha → 1, ravi → 2, meera → 1, kabir → 1. Partition 0 gets nothing: with few keys, hashing can be uneven.
A consumer group of 3 gives one consumer per partition, and the one on partition 0 sits idle. A fourth consumer would get no partition at all.
Events at seconds 5, 12, 58, 61, 75, 119, 120 and 130. Tumbling 60-second windows: [0, 60) holds 3, [60, 120) holds 3, [120, 180) holds 2.
Hopping windows 60 s wide, starting every 30 s: [0, 60) 3, [30, 90) 3, [60, 120) 3, [90, 150) 3, [120, 180) 2. Each event after second 30 is counted in two windows; 5 and 12 fall only in [0, 60).

A consumer adds payments of 100, 250, 80, 400, 120 and 60, a total of 1,010, but crashes after the fourth and fifth and before committing, so those two come again. A plain sum says 1,530; skipping event ids already seen keeps 1,010.

selftest.q: Kafka: 12 partitions and 15 consumers in one group. What happens?

selftest.q: Delivery is at-least-once. How do you keep the results correct?

selftest.q: Tumbling or hopping windows: what is the difference?
selftest.a: Tumbling windows are fixed and back to back, so each event falls in exactly one. Hopping windows have a fixed size but start more often than that, so they overlap: 60 s every 30 s puts each event in two.

blocks.title: Locking vs MVCC: how Postgres handles concurrent writes
blocks.builds_on: Day 82 · isolation levels and the anomalies they prevent, Day 75 · transactions and ACID, and Day 26 · a lock around a critical section
points: Two ways to keep transactions apart. Locking: a reader takes a shared lock and a writer an exclusive one, so readers and writers wait for each other. MVCC (multi-version concurrency control): a writer adds a new version of the row, and each reader sees the version its snapshot allows.

In Postgres every row version carries xmin, the transaction that created it, and xmax, the one that deleted or replaced it. An UPDATE doesn't overwrite: it sets the old version's xmax and writes a new version with a new xmin.

A snapshot records which transactions had committed when it was taken. A version is visible if its xmin had committed by then and its xmax hadn't. READ COMMITTED takes a new snapshot per statement; REPEATABLE READ keeps one for the whole transaction (Day 82).

So readers never block writers, and writers never block readers. Two writers on one row still clash: the second waits for the first's row lock, and if the first commits, at REPEATABLE READ the second then fails with a serialization failure and must retry.

SELECT … FOR UPDATE locks the rows it reads until commit, which makes read-then-write safe at READ COMMITTED: a second transaction's FOR UPDATE on that row waits. Book the last seat this way and the second buyer reads 0.

Old versions pile up until no snapshot can see them. VACUUM marks their space for reuse, and autovacuum runs it for you; VACUUM FULL rewrites the table to give space back to the disk, under a lock that blocks everything.

A transaction left open for hours, such as an idle connection or a long report, holds an old snapshot, so VACUUM can't clear anything that died after it began and the table bloats. Today's guide lesson covers exactly this, so the block's own reading is shorter.
MySQL's InnoDB is MVCC too, keeping old versions in an undo log rather than in the table. SQLite in WAL mode lets a reader keep its snapshot while one writer commits.
blocks.say: Postgres uses MVCC: an update writes a new row version stamped with xmin and xmax, and each reader sees the versions its snapshot allows, so reads and writes don't block each other; writers on the same row still wait on a row lock, SELECT FOR UPDATE takes that lock up front for read-then-write, and VACUUM clears versions no snapshot can see, which a long-open transaction holds back.
example: A wallet row with balance 500, created by transaction 100: xmin 100, no xmax.

Transaction 200, at REPEATABLE READ, starts and reads 500. Transaction 201 runs UPDATE … SET balance = 200 and commits: the old version gets xmax 201 and a new version (xmin 201, balance 200) is added. 201 never waited for 200.
200 reads again. Its snapshot was taken before 201 committed, so the new version is invisible to it and the old one still visible: 500. A transaction starting now reads 200.
Once 200 ends and no snapshot from before 201 is left, the 500 version is dead, and VACUUM marks its space for reuse.

Had 200 tried to update the row, it would have failed with "could not serialize access due to concurrent update". At READ COMMITTED it would instead wait for 201 to commit, then update the new version.

points: When a question asks which nodes can reach a target, a search forward from every node repeats the same work over and over. Turn the edges round and search backwards from the target instead: one search finds everything that can reach it. Each search is O(V + E).
Reversing the edges flips the rule too: if a move from a to b is allowed when a ≥ b, the backward search steps from b to a when a ≥ b.

Water flows to a neighbour that is lower or equal. Walking backwards from the ocean, which neighbours may you step to?
There are two oceans. How many backward searches do you run, and what do you do with the cells each one reaches?

blocks.say: Instead of testing every cell's path to the sea, I BFS or DFS inwards from each ocean's border cells, stepping only to neighbours at least as high, collect the two sets of reachable cells and return their intersection: O(rows × cols).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): a town's one-way streets run A→B, B→H, C→A, D→E, E→D and H→D. From which junctions can you drive to the hospital at H?
Forwards, you would search from each of the 6 junctions and see whether it reaches H: 6 searches.
Reverse every street: B→A, H→B, A→C, E→D, D→E and D→H. Search once from H: H, then B, then A, then C.
So H, B, A and C can reach the hospital. D and E can't: their streets only lead to each other.
One search on the reversed graph, O(V + E), replaced one search per junction.

Step 2: without the board, what state do you still need to know whether a square is safe? What does the base case return now?

blocks.say: I reuse N-Queens' row-by-row search with sets for columns, r − c and r + c, but return counts instead of building boards: row n returns 1 and each row sums its safe columns' counts, still about O(n!) time and O(n) space.
example: Practice problem (not NeetCode 250): how many orders of 1, 2, 3, 4 have no two consecutive numbers side by side, so no 1 next to 2, 2 next to 3, or 3 next to 4?
Count, don't list: count(path) returns how many ways this path can finish. Base case: all 4 placed, return 1. Otherwise add up count over each unused number that isn't 1 away from the last one.
Start 1: next is 3 or 4. After 1, 3 both 2 and 4 are 1 away from 3: dead. After 1, 4 only 2 fits, and then 3 is next to 2: dead. Start 1 gives 0.
Start 2: only 4 fits, then 1, then 3: one way, 2, 4, 1, 3. Start 3 mirrors it: 3, 1, 4, 2. Start 4 mirrors start 1: 0. Total 2.
Nothing was stored but the path: each call returns a number and its parent adds them up, so memory is O(n).

blocks.title: Design YouTube: upload, transcode and stream
blocks.builds_on: Day 74 · blob storage, presigned URLs, multipart upload and CDNs, Day 39 · message queues and workers, Day 88 · Kafka partitions and consumer groups, Day 20 · choosing a database, Day 41 · sharding, Day 11 · estimates, and Day 32 · the 45-minute design framework
points: The ask: users upload videos, and anyone can watch them smoothly, on a phone on 4G or a TV on fibre. Scope it: upload, processing, watching and view counts; leave comments, search and recommendations out unless asked.

Numbers (Day 11): 10 million daily users, of whom 5% upload one 300 MB video a day: 500,000 uploads and 150 TB of originals a day. Watching dwarfs uploading, so the design is read-heavy and bandwidth is the biggest bill.

Upload: the app asks the API for presigned URLs and sends the file straight to blob storage in parts, a multipart upload, so a dropped 4G connection resumes instead of restarting (Day 74). The API servers never carry the bytes.

Processing: when the upload completes, a message goes onto a queue (Day 39). Workers transcode the original into several renditions, such as 240p, 480p, 720p and 1080p, each cut into segments a few seconds long, plus thumbnails. A long video is split into chunks so many workers transcode it at once.

Streaming is adaptive: an HLS or DASH manifest lists each rendition's segments, and the player measures its bandwidth and picks a rendition for each next segment, dropping to 240p in a tunnel and climbing back after.
CDN: segments are files that never change, ideal for edge caching (Day 74). Popular videos stay at the edge; the long tail of rarely watched ones comes from blob storage on a miss.

Metadata, such as title, owner, status (uploading, processing, ready) and the manifest's URL, lives in a database sharded by video id (Days 20 and 41), with a cache in front. View counts go through a stream (Day 88): each play is an event, and a consumer adds them up per video per minute instead of running an UPDATE per view on one hot row.
Deep dives an interviewer may pick: resumable upload, transcoding cost and priority, the CDN bill, and how exact view counts must be versus how fresh.
blocks.say: Uploads go straight to blob storage through presigned multipart URLs, a queue drives transcoding workers that cut each video into HLS or DASH segments at several bitrates, the CDN serves the segments while the player picks a bitrate per segment, metadata sits in a sharded database with a cache, and view counts flow through a stream instead of hot-row updates.
example: Asha uploads a 300 MB cooking video from Pune. The API checks her login, writes a metadata row with status uploading, and returns presigned URLs for 30 parts of 10 MB.

Her phone sends the parts straight to blob storage. The connection drops during part 18, and the app resumes from part 18 instead of starting over. When the last part lands, an event goes onto the transcode queue.
Workers split the video into chunks, transcode them in parallel into 240p to 1080p segments of 4 seconds, write the manifests, and set the status to ready.

Ravi in Delhi presses play and the player fetches the manifest from the CDN. On 6.5 Mbps fibre it picks 1080p (5 Mbps); in a metro tunnel his bandwidth falls to 1.2 Mbps and the next segments come at 240p.
Each play sends a view event to the stream; a consumer adds them up per video per minute and writes one update a minute, so a viral video never hammers one row.

Day 32's first 15 minutes, on paper: requirements and estimates. Assume 10 million daily users, 5% upload one 300 MB video a day, and everyone watches 5 videos a day at about 50 MB each. Check: 500,000 uploads and 150 TB of originals a day, and 2.5 PB a day out of the CDN. At ₹1.5 per GB that is ₹37.5 lakh a day, so say which part of the design you would make cheaper first (the CDN bill).

About 20 minutes, in d90.py: `Upload(total_parts, queue)` with `put(part)` and `missing()`. put records a part, and when the last missing part arrives it appends one "transcode" event to queue, a plain list standing in for Day 39's queue; missing() returns the part numbers not yet received. Check: with 30 parts and parts 1 to 17 sent before the connection drops, missing() is 18 to 30, 13 parts; sending those makes queue ['transcode'], and sending part 30 again, a retry, still leaves one event.

About 10 minutes, in d90.py: write `pick(bandwidth_kbps)` that returns the highest rendition whose bitrate is at most 0.8 × the bandwidth, from 240p at 400, 480p at 1,000, 720p at 2,500 and 1080p at 5,000 kbps, and 240p if none fits. Check: 6,500 → 1080p, 3,500 → 720p, 1,200 → 240p, 800 → 240p, 4,000 → 720p. Say why the player keeps a 20% margin.

About 20 minutes: add `ViewCounter`, a consumer like Day 88's. `handle(event_id, video, t)` skips an event id it has already applied, then adds 1 to counts[(video, t // 60)]; `flush(minute)` returns {video: views} for that minute, one database write per video per minute. Feed it (1, "v1", 3), (2, "v2", 10), (3, "v1", 15), (4, "v1", 42), (5, "v1", 59), (6, "v1", 61), (7, "v2", 65), (8, "v1", 70), then (4, "v1", 42) and (5, "v1", 59) again, as after a crash before the commit. Check: flush(0) is {'v1': 4, 'v2': 1} and flush(1) is {'v1': 2, 'v2': 1}, so 10 events become 4 writes; without the id check, v1's first minute would say 6. Run it with `uv run python d90.py`.

About 8 minutes, out loud, then on paper: a creator uploads a 2-hour video. How do you make it watchable fast? Check: split it into chunks transcoded in parallel, and make the low renditions first, so it can go live at 240p and 480p while 1080p is still being made.

selftest.q: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow: why search from the oceans rather than from each cell?
selftest.a: One search inwards from each ocean's border, stepping to neighbours at least as high, finds every cell that drains into it: O(rows × cols) in all, instead of one search per cell.

selftest.q: N-Queens II: what changes from N-Queens?
selftest.a: Nothing is built: the recursion returns how many boards finish from this row, 1 at row n, and each row adds up the counts of its safe columns.

selftest.q: How does adaptive bitrate streaming work?
selftest.a: Each video is transcoded into several bitrates, cut into segments a few seconds long and listed in an HLS or DASH manifest. The player measures its bandwidth and picks the rendition for each next segment.

selftest.q: Why upload through presigned multipart URLs?
selftest.a: The bytes go straight to blob storage instead of through the API servers, and a dropped connection resumes from the last finished part instead of restarting the whole file.

selftest.q: Why do view counts go through a stream instead of an UPDATE per view?
selftest.a: A viral video's row would take thousands of writes a second. A consumer adds up the view events per video per minute and writes one update a minute.
